title: Complete Accounting & Bookkeeping Program
description: A full 20-module program from beginner to advanced: foundations, source documents, journals and ledgers, cash and bank records, sales and purchases, inventory, payroll, fixed assets, financial statements, cash flow and budgeting, cost accounting, taxation, organization types, internal controls and ethics, financial analysis, digital bookkeeping, careers and certification, hands-on projects, and a Certificate of Completion.
outcomes: Explain the difference between accounting and bookkeeping and apply the accounting equation
Record transactions using source documents, journals, ledgers and the trial balance
Maintain a cashbook, petty cash, and reconcile cash and bank balances
Handle sales, purchases, inventory, payroll, and fixed assets and depreciation
Prepare an income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow and budget reports
Apply cost accounting, taxation basics, and accounting for different organization types
Use internal controls, auditing awareness, ethics and financial ratio analysis
Keep digital, secure records in a spreadsheet and build a real bookkeeping career path
about: This is the complete TIH Accounting & Bookkeeping course, rebuilt into twenty modules that take you from absolute beginner foundations through advanced financial analysis, taxation, internal controls, and digital bookkeeping.

Every content lesson has an authored, easy-to-follow note (hook question, plain-English explanation, real-life relevance, try-it activity, key words and self-check questions) with its own short practice quiz; eight hands-on projects and a Capstone Bookkeeping File turn theory into real, usable records.

You finish with subject quizzes, a Midterm and Final Examination, and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion. Designed for entrepreneurs, office assistants, NGO and church administrators, students, and anyone who wants to manage money with confidence.
requirements: No accounting experience required, this course starts from the basics
A notebook, calculator, and phone or computer for practice
Willingness to practice with sample receipts, invoices, ledgers and spreadsheets

Welcome to the Program

Welcome to the Program is the focus of this Foundations of Accounting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain the purpose, users, branches, and foundational logic of accounting.

accounting

🤔 Let's start with a question
Every business, church, and family manages money. But only some of them can actually explain, clearly, where that money came from and where it went. Which kind do you want to be?

Welcome to the Program

In plain words

This course teaches you accounting and bookkeeping from the very beginning — the practical skills of recording, organising, and understanding money, whether for a business, a nonprofit, or your own household.

Think of this course as learning to read and write a language — the language of money. Once you're fluent, financial records that used to look like confusing numbers start telling you a clear, useful story.

What this program covers

StageWhat you'll learn
BeginnerCore concepts, recording transactions, cash and bank records
IntermediateFinancial statements, inventory, payroll, taxation
AdvancedCost accounting, financial analysis, auditing, digital tools
CapstoneBuilding a complete bookkeeping system from scratch

Why this matters to you

Every organisation — a shop, a school, a church, an NGO, or your own family budget — needs someone who can keep clear, honest financial records. Completing this program makes you that person.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write down one real reason YOU personally want to learn accounting and bookkeeping (a job, your own business, helping your church or family).

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
AccountingThe practice of recording, organising, and interpreting financial information
BookkeepingThe day-to-day recording of financial transactions
Study tip: Keep your personal reason for taking this course somewhere visible — it's a helpful reminder on the days the material feels difficult.

lessons.title: 1.2 What Is Accounting?
lessons.html:
What Is Accounting?Lesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Accounting?

What Is Accounting? is the focus of this Foundations of Accounting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain the purpose, users, branches, and foundational logic of accounting.

accounting

The process of recording, summarising, analysing, and communicating financial information.

bookkeeping

The systematic day-to-day recording of financial transactions.

financial information

Money-related data used to understand and manage an organisation.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop owner asks, “Am I actually making money this year, or just staying busy?” What kind of information would actually answer that question?

What Is Accounting?

In plain words

Accounting is the process of recording, summarising, and interpreting financial information so people can understand how an organisation is really performing and make good decisions.

Think of accounting like a health check-up: it doesn't just collect raw numbers (blood pressure, temperature), it interprets them into a clear picture of “how healthy is this business, really?”

The three core jobs of accounting

JobWhat it means
RecordingWriting down every financial transaction accurately
SummarisingOrganising those records into clear reports
InterpretingExplaining what the reports actually mean for decisions

Why this matters to you

Without accounting, a business owner is just guessing whether they're actually profitable — accounting turns that guess into a clear, evidence-based answer, which is exactly what banks, investors, and tax authorities also require.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a business you know (even a small shop). Write one question its owner might want accounting to answer, like “How much profit did I make this month?”

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
AccountingRecording, summarising, and interpreting financial information
Financial performanceHow well an organisation is doing financially over a period
Study tip: Whenever you see a financial report, ask “what decision is this actually helping someone make?” — that question is the real purpose behind every accounting report.

lessons.title: 1.3 What Is Bookkeeping?
lessons.html:
What Is Bookkeeping?Lesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Bookkeeping?

What Is Bookkeeping? is the focus of this Foundations of Accounting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain the purpose, users, branches, and foundational logic of accounting.

accounting

The process of recording, summarising, analysing, and communicating financial information.

bookkeeping

The systematic day-to-day recording of financial transactions.

financial information

Money-related data used to understand and manage an organisation.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Every single sale, purchase, and payment a business makes — does anyone actually write all of that down, every single day?

What Is Bookkeeping?

In plain words

Bookkeeping is the day-to-day task of recording every financial transaction as it happens — every sale, every purchase, every payment — accurately and consistently.

Bookkeeping is like keeping a detailed diary of every coin that moves in or out — not analysing it yet, just faithfully writing down exactly what happened, when, and how much.

What a bookkeeper actually records

Transaction typeExample
SalesA customer pays for goods or services
PurchasesThe business buys supplies or stock
PaymentsRent, wages, or a supplier's bill is paid
ReceiptsMoney is received from a customer or loan

Why this matters to you

Bookkeeping is the foundation everything else in this course is built on — accounting reports, tax filings, and business decisions are only as accurate as the day-to-day bookkeeping records they're built from.

🧪 Try it yourself: For one full day, mentally track (or actually write down) every time money changed hands around you — at a shop, at home, anywhere.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
TransactionA single event involving the exchange of money or value
BookkeeperThe person responsible for recording day-to-day financial transactions
Study tip: Record transactions the same day they happen whenever possible — waiting even a few days makes details much easier to forget or record wrongly.

lessons.title: 1.4 Accounting vs Bookkeeping
lessons.html:
Accounting vs BookkeepingLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Accounting vs Bookkeeping

Accounting vs Bookkeeping is the focus of this Foundations of Accounting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain the purpose, users, branches, and foundational logic of accounting.

accounting

The process of recording, summarising, analysing, and communicating financial information.

bookkeeping

The systematic day-to-day recording of financial transactions.

financial information

Money-related data used to understand and manage an organisation.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Two people at the same small business: one records every receipt daily, the other prepares the year-end report explaining if the business made a profit. Are they doing the same job?

Accounting vs Bookkeeping

In plain words

Bookkeeping is the day-to-day recording of transactions, while accounting uses those records to summarise, interpret, and report on the organisation's overall financial performance.

If bookkeeping is collecting every individual puzzle piece carefully, accounting is assembling those pieces into the full picture and explaining what that picture actually shows.

Comparing the two roles

BookkeepingAccounting
Main taskRecording transactions dailySummarising and interpreting records
TimingOngoing, every dayUsually periodic (monthly, yearly)
OutputOrganised transaction recordsReports like profit & loss, balance sheet

Why this matters to you

Understanding this difference helps you know exactly which skill you're using at any moment in this course — and later, it helps you know exactly which task to focus on first when managing real financial records.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take one transaction (like buying office supplies) and describe: what would the BOOKKEEPING record of it look like, versus what an ACCOUNTING report might later say about it?

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
PeriodicHappening regularly at set intervals, like monthly or yearly
Financial reportA summarised document explaining financial performance, built from bookkeeping records
Study tip: In a small business, one person often does both jobs — but mentally separating “recording” from “interpreting” still helps you do each task more clearly and carefully.

lessons.title: 1.5 Users of Financial Information
lessons.html:
Users of Financial InformationLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Users of Financial Information

Users of Financial Information is the focus of this Foundations of Accounting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain the purpose, users, branches, and foundational logic of accounting.

accounting

The process of recording, summarising, analysing, and communicating financial information.

bookkeeping

The systematic day-to-day recording of financial transactions.

financial information

Money-related data used to understand and manage an organisation.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business prepares a financial report. Is the owner really the only person who will ever read it?

Users of Financial Information

In plain words

Users of financial information are all the different people and organisations — inside and outside a business — who rely on financial records to make decisions.

Financial information is like a shared weather forecast — the same report is read by many different people (farmers, travellers, event planners), each using the same information to make their own different decisions.

Common users and what they need

UserWhy they need financial information
Owners/managersTo make day-to-day and strategic decisions
Banks/lendersTo decide whether to approve a loan
Tax authoritiesTo confirm the correct tax is being paid
EmployeesTo judge job security and negotiate pay
Donors (for NGOs)To confirm funds are being used properly

Why this matters to you

Knowing who actually reads financial records changes how you prepare them — a report for a bank loan application needs different emphasis than an internal report just for the owner's own planning.

🧪 Try it yourself: Pick one user from the table above and write one specific question they might ask when looking at a business's financial records.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
StakeholderAny person or group with an interest in an organisation's financial performance
External userSomeone outside the organisation who still needs its financial information, like a bank
Study tip: Before preparing any financial report, ask “who is actually going to read this, and what do they need to know?” — it shapes what you should emphasise.

lessons.title: 1.6 Branches of Accounting
lessons.html:
Branches of AccountingLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Branches of Accounting

Branches of Accounting is the focus of this Foundations of Accounting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain the purpose, users, branches, and foundational logic of accounting.

accounting

The process of recording, summarising, analysing, and communicating financial information.

bookkeeping

The systematic day-to-day recording of financial transactions.

financial information

Money-related data used to understand and manage an organisation.

🤔 Let's start with a question
“Accounting” sounds like one single job. But does preparing a tax return really require the exact same skills as investigating suspected fraud?

Branches of Accounting

In plain words

Accounting has several distinct branches — including financial, management, cost, tax, and auditing accounting — each focused on a different purpose.

Think of “accounting” like “medicine” — a broad field with distinct specialities (a surgeon, a dentist, a pharmacist) that all relate to health, but each requiring its own specific focus and skills.

Major branches of accounting

BranchMain focus
Financial accountingPreparing reports for external users (banks, investors)
Management accountingProviding information for internal business decisions
Cost accountingTracking and controlling the cost of producing goods/services
Tax accountingPreparing records and filings for tax compliance
AuditingIndependently checking that financial records are accurate and honest

Why this matters to you

This whole course will touch on several of these branches — recognising which branch a particular skill belongs to helps you understand not just HOW to do something, but WHY it matters for that specific purpose.

🧪 Try it yourself: Match each branch in the table above to one specific job title you think might use it (like “tax accountant” or “internal auditor”).

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Branch of accountingA specialised area within the broader field of accounting
ComplianceMeeting legal or regulatory requirements, like correct tax filing
Study tip: As you move through this course, notice which branch each new topic belongs to — it helps organise everything you're learning into a clearer overall map.

lessons.title: 1.7 The Accounting Equation
lessons.html:
The Accounting EquationLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Accounting Equation

The Accounting Equation is the focus of this Foundations of Accounting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain the purpose, users, branches, and foundational logic of accounting.

accounting

The process of recording, summarising, analysing, and communicating financial information.

bookkeeping

The systematic day-to-day recording of financial transactions.

financial information

Money-related data used to understand and manage an organisation.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business owns a car worth $10,000, but still owes $6,000 on a loan for it. How much of that car does the owner actually, truly own?

The Accounting Equation

In plain words

The accounting equation — Assets = Liabilities + Equity — shows that everything a business owns was funded either by borrowing or by the owner's own investment.

Think of the accounting equation like a house purchase: the house (asset) was paid for partly with a mortgage (liability) and partly with your own deposit (equity) — add those two funding sources together, and you get the full value of the house.

Breaking down the equation

TermMeaningExample
AssetsWhat the business ownsCash, equipment, inventory
LiabilitiesWhat the business owesLoans, unpaid bills
EquityThe owner's own stakeMoney invested + retained profit

Why this matters to you

This single equation is the foundation of every financial statement you'll build in this course — the balance sheet, in particular, is really just this equation written out in more detail.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using the example in the hook (a $10,000 car with a $6,000 loan), calculate the owner's actual equity in that car using the accounting equation.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
AssetSomething a business owns that has value
LiabilitySomething a business owes to someone else
EquityThe owner's own stake in the business, after liabilities are subtracted
Study tip: Whenever you're confused about a financial statement later in this course, come back to this simple equation — nearly everything else builds directly on top of it.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: The Accounting Equation

questions.explanation: The accounting equation states that assets equal liabilities plus equity.

questions.question: What does “equity” represent?

lessons.title: 2.1 Source Documents
lessons.html:
Source DocumentsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Source Documents

Source Documents is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A bookkeeper writes “sold goods, $200” in a ledger. If someone later asks “prove it,” what would they actually show?

Source Documents

In plain words

Source documents are the original paper or digital records — receipts, invoices, vouchers — that provide proof a transaction actually happened.

A source document is like a photograph taken at the exact moment something happened — without it, a written record is just someone's claim, with no actual evidence backing it up.

Common source documents

DocumentWhat it proves
ReceiptPayment was made or received
InvoiceA sale was made and payment is owed
Payment voucherAn internal payment was authorised and made
Bank statementMoney actually moved through the bank account

Why this matters to you

No transaction should ever be recorded in the books without a genuine source document behind it — this single discipline is what makes financial records trustworthy enough for banks, auditors, and tax authorities to actually rely on.

🧪 Try it yourself: Collect (or picture) three real source documents from your own recent spending — a receipt, a bill, or a bank message — and identify what each one proves.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Source documentAn original record providing evidence that a transaction occurred
EvidenceProof supporting that a transaction genuinely happened
Study tip: Keep every source document, even small ones — a missing receipt can make it impossible to prove a transaction happened months later.

lessons.title: 2.2 Receipts and Invoices
lessons.html:
Receipts and InvoicesLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Receipts and Invoices

Receipts and Invoices is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A customer says “I already paid you last week.” Without paperwork, how would you actually confirm whether that's true?

Receipts and Invoices

In plain words

A receipt confirms that payment has already been made, while an invoice requests payment that is still owed.

An invoice is like a bill handed to you at a restaurant — a request for payment. A receipt is like the stamped proof you get afterward — confirmation that the payment actually happened.

Receipts vs. invoices

ReceiptInvoice
PurposeConfirms payment already receivedRequests payment still owed
Given whenAfter payment is madeBefore or at the time of a sale
Key detailsDate, amount, payer, reasonCustomer, items, price, due date

Why this matters to you

Confusing these two documents is a common bookkeeping mistake — issuing a “receipt” for money you haven't actually received yet creates a false, misleading record.

🧪 Try it yourself: Create a simple sample invoice (for an imaginary $50 sale) and a matching sample receipt once that payment is received, including all the key details from the table.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
ReceiptA document confirming that payment has already been received
InvoiceA document requesting payment that is still owed
Study tip: Never issue a receipt until payment has genuinely been received — a receipt is a confirmation of fact, not a hopeful prediction.

lessons.title: 2.3 Payment Vouchers
lessons.html:
Payment VouchersLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Payment Vouchers

Payment Vouchers is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
An organisation's cashier is about to pay a supplier $300. Should they just hand over the cash, or does something need to happen first?

Payment Vouchers

In plain words

A payment voucher is an internal document used to authorise and record a payment before or as it is made, showing who approved it and why.

A payment voucher is like a signed permission slip before an important action — it creates a clear record of who approved the payment, for what reason, before the money actually leaves the organisation.

What a payment voucher includes

FieldPurpose
Date and amountExactly when and how much was paid
Reason for paymentWhat the payment is actually for
Approving signatureWho authorised the payment
Supporting document referenceLinks to the invoice or bill being paid

Why this matters to you

Requiring a payment voucher for every payment — especially in organisations with more than one person handling money — creates a clear approval trail that protects against mistakes and misuse of funds.

🧪 Try it yourself: Design a simple payment voucher template with the four fields from the table above, ready to use for a real or practice payment.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Payment voucherAn internal document authorising and recording a payment
Approval trailA clear record showing who approved each payment and why
Study tip: Always require a payment voucher approval BEFORE money is paid, not after — this order is what actually gives the control its protective value.

lessons.title: 2.4 The Accounting Cycle
lessons.html:
The Accounting CycleLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Accounting Cycle

The Accounting Cycle is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
From the moment a sale happens to the moment it appears correctly on a year-end financial report — how many actual steps happen in between?

The Accounting Cycle

In plain words

The accounting cycle is the repeating sequence of steps a business follows to record transactions and turn them into finished financial reports.

The accounting cycle is like a factory production line — raw material (a transaction) enters at one end, passes through several defined stages, and comes out the other end as a finished product (a financial report).

The main stages of the cycle

StageWhat happens
1. Identify transactionsRecognise a financial event has occurred
2. Record in journalsWrite the transaction down in order
3. Post to ledgersOrganise transactions by account
4. Prepare trial balanceCheck that debits and credits balance
5. Prepare financial statementsSummarise the period's overall performance

Why this matters to you

Every topic in the next several modules of this course — journals, ledgers, trial balances — is really just one specific stage of this same repeating cycle, so understanding the whole cycle now gives you a map for everything coming next.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take one transaction (like a cash sale) and briefly describe what would happen to it at each of the five stages above.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Accounting cycleThe repeating sequence of steps turning transactions into financial reports
Trial balanceA check confirming that total debits equal total credits
Study tip: Whenever you learn a new bookkeeping skill in this course, ask “which stage of the accounting cycle does this belong to?” — it keeps everything connected in your mind.

questions.explanation: Seeing the full cycle helps a learner understand how each specific skill fits into the larger, connected process.

lessons.title: 2.5 Chart of Accounts
lessons.html:
Chart of AccountsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Chart of Accounts

Chart of Accounts is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business has hundreds of transactions a month. Without some kind of organising system, how would anyone find “total rent paid this year” quickly?

Chart of Accounts

In plain words

A chart of accounts is an organised list of every account category a business uses to record its financial transactions, like Cash, Sales, Rent, and Loans.

A chart of accounts is like a labelled filing cabinet with a drawer for every category — instead of throwing every transaction into one giant pile, each one goes into its own clearly labelled drawer.

Typical account categories

CategoryExample accounts
AssetsCash, Equipment, Inventory
LiabilitiesLoans Payable, Accounts Payable
EquityOwner's Capital, Retained Earnings
IncomeSales Revenue, Service Income
ExpensesRent Expense, Wages Expense

Why this matters to you

A well-organised chart of accounts makes every later step — journals, ledgers, financial statements — dramatically easier, since every transaction already has a clear, correct “drawer” to be filed into.

🧪 Try it yourself: Create a simple chart of accounts for a small business you can imagine (like a shop), listing at least one account under each of the five categories above.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Chart of accountsAn organised list of account categories used to record transactions
Account categoryA broad group like Assets, Liabilities, or Expenses, containing individual accounts
Study tip: Set up your chart of accounts carefully at the very start of any new bookkeeping system — reorganising it later, after many transactions are already recorded, is far more difficult.

lessons.title: 2.6 Double-Entry Bookkeeping
lessons.html:
Double-Entry BookkeepingLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Double-Entry Bookkeeping

Double-Entry Bookkeeping is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business pays $100 cash for supplies. Does that transaction really only affect ONE thing (the cash), or does it actually affect two things at once?

Double-Entry Bookkeeping

In plain words

Double-entry bookkeeping means every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts — one account increases while another decreases, always keeping the accounting equation in balance.

Double-entry is like a seesaw: whenever one side goes up, the other side must go down by the same amount, so the whole system always stays perfectly balanced, no matter how many transactions happen.

How double-entry works

TransactionAccount 1 effectAccount 2 effect
Buy supplies for cashSupplies (asset) increasesCash (asset) decreases
Take out a bank loanCash (asset) increasesLoan (liability) increases
Pay rent in cashRent expense increasesCash (asset) decreases

Why this matters to you

Double-entry bookkeeping is the single most important concept in this entire course — nearly every remaining topic (journals, ledgers, trial balances) exists specifically to correctly apply this one core idea.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take the “buy supplies for cash” example and explain, in your own words, why BOTH accounts change, not just one.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Double-entryA system where every transaction affects at least two accounts
BalanceThe state where total debits equal total credits across all accounts
Study tip: Whenever you record a transaction, ask “what are the TWO effects here?” — training yourself to always look for the second effect prevents the most common bookkeeping errors.

questions.explanation: Journals, ledgers, and trial balances are all built around correctly applying the double-entry principle.

lessons.title: 2.7 Debits and Credits
lessons.html:
Debits and CreditsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Debits and Credits

Debits and Credits is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
“Debit” and “credit” sound like simple words for “subtract” and “add.” Is it really that simple in accounting?

Debits and Credits

In plain words

Debits and credits are the two sides of every double-entry transaction — which one increases or decreases an account depends on what TYPE of account it is.

Debits and credits are like left and right hands working together — neither is inherently “good” or “bad,” “increase” or “decrease”; their actual effect depends entirely on which type of account they're touching.

How debits and credits affect each account type

Account typeDebit effectCredit effect
AssetsIncreaseDecrease
LiabilitiesDecreaseIncrease
EquityDecreaseIncrease
IncomeDecreaseIncrease
ExpensesIncreaseDecrease

Why this matters to you

This single table is something you'll refer back to constantly throughout the rest of this course — memorising it thoroughly now makes every future journal entry and ledger posting far faster and more confident.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using the table above, work out: if a business receives cash from a customer (an income transaction), does Cash get debited or credited? Does Income get debited or credited?

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
DebitAn entry on the left side of an account, with an effect depending on account type
CreditAn entry on the right side of an account, with an effect depending on account type
Study tip: Memorise this table (“DEAD CLIC”: Debit Expenses, Assets, Drawings increase; Credit Liabilities, Income, Capital increase) — it's one of the most useful memory aids in all of bookkeeping.

options: It increases the account

lessons.title: 2.8 T-Accounts
lessons.html:
T-AccountsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

T-Accounts

T-Accounts is the focus of this Source Documents & The Accounting Cycle lesson. It develops the learner's ability to trace transactions through source documents and the accounting cycle.

source document

Original evidence that a financial transaction occurred.

double entry

A system recording equal debit and credit effects for every transaction.

chart of accounts

An organised list of account names and codes.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You need to quickly see all the debits and credits for the “Cash” account, side by side. Is there a simple way to visualise that, before using a full ledger page?

T-Accounts

In plain words

A T-account is a simple visual tool shaped like the letter “T,” with debits recorded on the left side and credits on the right, used to see an account's activity at a glance.

A T-account is like a simple scoreboard with two columns — one side tracking every point added, the other every point subtracted — letting you see the whole game's activity for one specific account instantly.

The structure of a T-account

Left side (Debit)Account NameRight side (Credit)
Amounts debitede.g. “Cash”Amounts credited
Increases (for assets)Decreases (for assets)

Why this matters to you

T-accounts are a genuinely useful learning and quick-reference tool — many bookkeepers still sketch a quick T-account by hand to check their thinking before recording a transaction in the full, formal ledger.

🧪 Try it yourself: Draw a T-account for “Cash” and record two transactions in it: cash received from a sale (debit) and cash paid for rent (credit).

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
T-accountA simple visual tool showing debits on the left and credits on the right for one account
Account balanceThe difference between the total debits and total credits in an account
Study tip: Sketch a quick T-account by hand whenever you're unsure how a transaction should be recorded — it's a fast, simple way to check your own thinking before committing it to the formal books.

lessons.title: 3.1 The General Journal
lessons.html:
The General JournalLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The General Journal

The General Journal is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business makes fifteen different transactions in one day. Where does the very first, raw record of each one actually get written down?

The General Journal

In plain words

The general journal is the book (physical or digital) where every transaction is first recorded, in date order, before being organised anywhere else.

The general journal is like a daily diary — every single event goes in, in the order it happened, before you later organise those entries by topic elsewhere.

What a journal entry includes

ElementPurpose
DateWhen the transaction happened
Accounts affectedWhich accounts are debited and credited
AmountsHow much money is involved
NarrationA short description explaining the transaction

Why this matters to you

The general journal is the true starting point of the entire accounting cycle — every ledger, trial balance, and financial statement that comes later ultimately traces back to an entry that was first made here.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write one simple journal entry for a transaction like “paid $50 cash for office supplies,” including the date, accounts, amounts, and a short narration.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Journal entryA single recorded transaction, showing the accounts debited and credited
NarrationA brief description explaining what a journal entry is for
Study tip: Always include a clear narration with every journal entry — without it, even you might not remember months later exactly why a transaction was recorded.

lessons.title: 3.2 Journalizing Transactions
lessons.html:
Journalizing TransactionsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Journalizing Transactions

Journalizing Transactions is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You know a journal entry needs a date, accounts, amounts, and a narration. But how do you actually decide WHICH accounts to debit and credit for a real transaction?

Journalizing Transactions

In plain words

Journalizing is the process of analysing a transaction and correctly recording it as a journal entry, using the debit and credit rules.

Journalizing is like translating a real event into the specific “language” of accounting — the event itself (buying supplies) stays the same, but you must translate it correctly into the accounts, debits, and credits that represent it.

Steps to journalize a transaction

StepQuestion to ask
1. Identify the accounts involvedWhat two (or more) accounts does this transaction touch?
2. Identify the account typesIs each one an asset, liability, equity, income, or expense?
3. Apply debit/credit rulesDoes each account increase or decrease, and by which side?
4. Write the entryRecord the date, accounts, amounts, and narration

Why this matters to you

Journalizing correctly is the single skill that determines whether everything built afterward — ledgers, trial balances, financial statements — is accurate or wrong from the very start.

🧪 Try it yourself: Journalize this transaction step by step: “Received $500 cash from a customer for services provided.”

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
JournalizeTo analyse and record a transaction as a formal journal entry
Account typeWhether an account is an asset, liability, equity, income, or expense
Study tip: Practice journalizing simple, everyday transactions regularly — this step-by-step habit becomes fast and automatic with repetition, much like learning to type.

lessons.title: 3.3 The General Ledger
lessons.html:
The General LedgerLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The General Ledger

The General Ledger is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You've journalized fifty separate transactions this month. How do you quickly find the TOTAL activity for just the “Cash” account, out of all fifty entries?

The General Ledger

In plain words

The general ledger organises every journal entry by account, so you can see all the activity — and the running balance — for one specific account at a time.

If the journal is a diary listing events in the order they happened, the ledger is like sorting that same diary into separate folders by topic — one folder for “Cash,” one for “Rent,” and so on.

Journal vs. ledger

JournalLedger
Organised byDate (chronological order)Account (grouped by category)
ShowsEvery transaction as it happenedAll activity for one specific account
Used forThe first, raw recordUnderstanding one account's full history and balance

Why this matters to you

Without the ledger, understanding “how much rent have we paid this year in total?” would mean manually searching through every single journal entry — the ledger organises that same information instantly by account.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take three journal entries you've written in this course so far and organise them into a simple ledger, grouped by account.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
General ledgerA record organising all transactions by account, showing each account's activity and balance
Running balanceThe current total of an account, updated after each new transaction
Study tip: Think of the ledger as the journal's information “re-sorted” for a different purpose — same transactions, organised by account instead of by date, for a different kind of question.

lessons.title: 3.4 Posting to the Ledger
lessons.html:
Posting to the LedgerLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Posting to the Ledger

Posting to the Ledger is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You've written a journal entry. Does it magically appear in the ledger by itself, or does someone need to actually move it there?

Posting to the Ledger

In plain words

Posting is the process of transferring each journal entry into its correct accounts in the general ledger.

Posting is like sorting mail after it arrives — the journal is the mailbox where everything first lands, and posting is the act of physically placing each letter into its correct labelled folder.

Steps to post a journal entry

StepWhat to do
1. Take the journal entryStart with a completed, correct journal entry
2. Find each account in the ledgerLocate the specific account page for each account involved
3. Record the amountEnter the debit or credit amount in that account
4. Update the running balanceRecalculate that account's new total

Why this matters to you

Posting must be done accurately and completely — a journal entry that is only half-posted (one account updated, the other forgotten) breaks the fundamental double-entry balance the whole system depends on.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take a simple journal entry (like “Cash increases $100, Sales increases $100”) and manually post both sides into two separate T-accounts.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
PostingTransferring a journal entry into its correct ledger accounts
Ledger accountThe specific page or section in the ledger for one account, like Cash
Study tip: After posting any entry, always double-check that BOTH sides were posted — a common and serious error is updating one account correctly and simply forgetting the other.

lessons.title: 3.5 Subsidiary Ledgers
lessons.html:
Subsidiary LedgersLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Subsidiary Ledgers

Subsidiary Ledgers is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business has 200 different customers who owe money. Does the main general ledger really need one giant, cluttered list of all 200 individually?

Subsidiary Ledgers

In plain words

A subsidiary ledger is a detailed, separate ledger for a specific group of related accounts, like individual customers or suppliers, that supports one summary account in the general ledger.

A subsidiary ledger is like a detailed appendix supporting a book's short summary chapter — the general ledger shows one clean total, while the underlying detail for every individual customer lives separately, easily accessible when needed.

Common subsidiary ledgers

Subsidiary ledgerTracksSupports which general ledger account
Accounts receivable ledgerIndividual customers who owe moneyAccounts Receivable (one total)
Accounts payable ledgerIndividual suppliers owed moneyAccounts Payable (one total)

Why this matters to you

Subsidiary ledgers let a business keep the main general ledger clean and simple (one total figure) while still having full, detailed records for every individual customer or supplier readily available when needed.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine three customers who each owe your business a different amount. Set up a simple subsidiary ledger listing each one, and check that their total matches what a single “Accounts Receivable” line would show.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Subsidiary ledgerA detailed ledger for a related group of accounts, supporting one general ledger total
Control accountThe general ledger account (like Accounts Receivable) that a subsidiary ledger's total must match
Study tip: Regularly check that a subsidiary ledger's total matches its corresponding general ledger account exactly — a mismatch is an early warning sign of a recording error somewhere.

lessons.title: 3.6 The Trial Balance
lessons.html:
The Trial BalanceLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Trial Balance

The Trial Balance is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You've posted dozens of journal entries across many accounts. Is there a quick way to check whether you've made a basic recording mistake somewhere?

The Trial Balance

In plain words

A trial balance lists every account and its balance, checking that total debits equal total credits across the whole ledger.

A trial balance is like counting the total money on both sides of a set of scales — if both sides don't match, you know immediately that something has gone wrong somewhere, even without yet knowing exactly where.

How to prepare a trial balance

StepWhat to do
1. List every accountEvery account from the ledger, with its current balance
2. Place in debit or credit columnBased on whether it's a debit or credit balance
3. Total both columnsAdd up all the debit balances and all the credit balances
4. Compare the totalsThey should be exactly equal

Why this matters to you

A trial balance doesn't catch every possible mistake (like a transaction posted to the wrong account entirely), but it reliably catches many basic errors — an unequal trial balance is a clear, unmissable signal that something needs correcting before moving forward.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using any three accounts and balances you've practised with in this course, build a simple trial balance and confirm the two columns are equal.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Trial balanceA list of all accounts and balances, checking that total debits equal total credits
Out of balanceWhen a trial balance's debit and credit totals do not match
Study tip: Prepare a trial balance regularly, not just at year-end — catching an imbalance early, while there are fewer transactions to check, makes finding the actual error far easier.

lessons.title: 3.7 Correcting Errors
lessons.html:
Correcting ErrorsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Correcting Errors

Correcting Errors is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You discover a transaction was recorded in the wrong account last month, after several other entries were already added on top of it. Can you just erase and rewrite it?

Correcting Errors

In plain words

Correcting errors in bookkeeping means fixing mistakes properly, using a traceable correcting entry, rather than erasing or altering the original record.

A proper correction is like crossing out a mistake in a signed legal document and initialling the correction, rather than using correction fluid to hide it — the fix should be visible and traceable, not hidden.

How to correct an error properly

StepWhy it matters
Identify the exact errorKnow precisely what was recorded wrong
Never erase the original entryKeeps a clear, honest audit trail
Record a correcting journal entryReverses the mistake and records it correctly
Add a clear narrationExplains why the correction was made

Why this matters to you

Never erasing or altering original entries isn't just good practice — in many organisations it's a genuine requirement, since a clear correction trail is exactly what protects a business during an audit or investigation.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine you recorded a $50 payment as “Office Supplies” by mistake, when it should have been “Rent Expense.” Write the correcting journal entry needed to fix this properly.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Correcting entryA new journal entry that fixes a previous recording error without erasing it
Audit trailA clear, traceable history of every entry and correction made
Study tip: Treat every correction as its own properly documented entry — this habit protects your credibility and the organisation's if records are ever formally reviewed.

lessons.title: 3.8 Suspense Accounts
lessons.html:
Suspense AccountsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Suspense Accounts

Suspense Accounts is the focus of this Journals and Ledgers lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record, post, balance, and correct accounting entries.

journal

A chronological book of original entry.

ledger

A collection of individual accounts showing transaction effects.

trial balance

A list used to check whether total debits equal total credits.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Your trial balance is out of balance by exactly $40, but you can't immediately find the specific error. Do you just leave the whole trial balance incomplete?

Suspense Accounts

In plain words

A suspense account is a temporary holding account used to keep a trial balance balanced while you investigate and locate the actual source of an error.

A suspense account is like a temporary “unresolved” tray on a desk — instead of losing track of a discrepancy or forcing an artificial fix, you set it aside clearly labelled until you have time to identify exactly what it is.

Using a suspense account

StepWhat happens
1. Trial balance doesn't balanceThere's a difference between total debits and credits
2. Post the difference to SuspenseTemporarily forces the trial balance to balance
3. Investigate the actual causeSearch for the specific error causing the imbalance
4. Correct and clear the suspense accountOnce found, the real correcting entry replaces the suspense entry

Why this matters to you

A suspense account should always be treated as temporary and urgent — it exists specifically to be investigated and cleared, not as a permanent place to quietly hide an unresolved discrepancy.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine your trial balance is $40 out of balance. Describe what you would post to the suspense account, and what your next step would be.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Suspense accountA temporary account holding an unexplained difference until it is investigated
DiscrepancyA difference between two figures that should otherwise match
Study tip: Review any suspense account balance regularly and treat it as an urgent task — a growing, unresolved suspense balance is a warning sign that real errors are accumulating unaddressed.

questions.explanation: Once identified, the true correcting entry is recorded, clearing the temporary suspense account balance.

lessons.title: 4.1 Cash Receipts
lessons.html:
Cash ReceiptsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cash Receipts

Cash Receipts is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A customer hands your shop physical cash for a purchase. Beyond just putting it in the till, what actually needs to happen for good record-keeping?

Cash Receipts

In plain words

A cash receipt is any money received by a business, and recording it properly means capturing the amount, date, source, and reason every single time.

Recording cash receipts is like a lifeguard keeping a headcount at a pool — you need an accurate, ongoing count of exactly what's come in, not just a vague sense that “business is good.”

What to record for every cash receipt

DetailWhy it matters
Date receivedPlaces the transaction in the correct time period
AmountThe exact figure received
SourceWho or what the money came from
ReasonWhat the payment was actually for

Why this matters to you

Every cash receipt should be recorded the moment it happens and matched to a source document (like a receipt issued to the customer) — this is the very first practical step that starts the whole accounting cycle for that piece of income.

🧪 Try it yourself: For one day, track every cash receipt you personally receive or observe (even small ones), noting the amount, source, and reason for each.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash receiptMoney received by a business, recorded with its amount, source, and reason
SourceWhere money received actually came from
Study tip: Record cash receipts immediately, not at the end of the day from memory — even a short delay increases the risk of forgetting a detail or an entire transaction.

lessons.title: 4.2 Cash Payments
lessons.html:
Cash PaymentsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cash Payments

Cash Payments is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Cash leaves a business constantly — rent, supplies, small errands. Is tracking money going OUT just as important as tracking money coming in?

Cash Payments

In plain words

A cash payment is any money paid out by a business, and recording it properly captures the amount, date, recipient, and reason for every payment.

If cash receipts are water flowing into a tank, cash payments are water flowing out — you need to track both directions accurately to actually know how much is left inside at any moment.

What to record for every cash payment

DetailWhy it matters
Date paidPlaces the payment in the correct time period
AmountThe exact figure paid out
RecipientWho or what received the payment
ReasonWhat the payment was actually for

Why this matters to you

Recording cash payments as carefully as cash receipts prevents one of the most common bookkeeping failures — a business that tracks income closely but lets outgoing cash slip by unrecorded, losing sight of where its money is actually going.

🧪 Try it yourself: List every cash payment you personally made yesterday (even a small one, like transport), and note the amount, recipient, and reason for each.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash paymentMoney paid out by a business, recorded with its amount, recipient, and reason
RecipientWho or what actually received a payment
Study tip: Keep even small cash payments (like transport or snacks bought for the office) properly recorded — small, unrecorded payments add up to a surprisingly large, untracked amount over a year.

lessons.title: 4.3 The Cashbook
lessons.html:
The CashbookLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Cashbook

The Cashbook is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business receives and pays cash constantly throughout the day. Is there one single, simple record that tracks both directions together?

The Cashbook

In plain words

A cashbook is a single record that tracks both cash received and cash paid, showing a running balance of how much cash the business actually has.

A cashbook is like a personal chequebook register — every deposit and withdrawal is logged in order, so at any moment you can see exactly how much money should actually be there.

Structure of a simple cashbook

ColumnPurpose
DateWhen the transaction happened
DescriptionWhat the transaction was for
Money inCash received
Money outCash paid
BalanceRunning total after each transaction

Why this matters to you

A well-maintained cashbook is one of the most practical, immediately useful tools in this entire course — even a very small business or church can maintain one confidently, without needing any accounting software at all.

🧪 Try it yourself: Create a simple cashbook with the five columns above and record three transactions (two receipts, one payment), keeping a running balance after each one.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
CashbookA single record tracking both cash received and cash paid, with a running balance
Running balanceThe updated total after each new cash transaction is recorded
Study tip: Update your cashbook the same day transactions happen, and total it regularly (like weekly) — a cashbook left unchecked for a long time becomes far harder to fix if an error creeps in.

lessons.title: 4.4 Petty Cash
lessons.html:
Petty CashLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Petty Cash

Petty Cash is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
An office needs $5 for stationery right now. Does someone really need to go through a full formal payment process for such a tiny amount?

Petty Cash

In plain words

Petty cash is a small amount of cash kept on hand to cover minor, everyday expenses without needing the full formal payment process each time.

Petty cash is like a small jar of coins kept in a kitchen for quick, minor needs — convenient for small, frequent purchases, but still counted and tracked carefully, not just left unmanaged.

Managing petty cash properly

PracticeWhy it matters
Set a fixed petty cash amountKeeps the fund small and manageable
Require a receipt for every useEven small payments need proof
Keep a petty cash logTracks every payment made from the fund
Reconcile regularlyConfirms the physical cash matches the recorded log

Why this matters to you

Petty cash is convenient specifically because it's small and simple — but that same convenience is exactly why it needs consistent discipline; small, casual amounts are also the easiest funds to quietly misuse if no one is tracking them.

🧪 Try it yourself: Design a simple petty cash log with columns for date, item, amount, and remaining balance, and record two small imaginary purchases.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Petty cashA small cash fund kept on hand for minor, everyday expenses
Petty cash logA record tracking every payment made from the petty cash fund
Study tip: Never let petty cash be used without a receipt, however small the amount — this single habit is what keeps a convenient system from quietly becoming an easy target for misuse.

lessons.title: 4.5 The Imprest System
lessons.html:
The Imprest SystemLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Imprest System

The Imprest System is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
An office's petty cash fund is meant to always hold $100. After spending $30, does someone just leave $70 in the box, or does something else happen?

The Imprest System

In plain words

The imprest system is a method for managing petty cash where the fund is regularly topped back up to its original fixed amount, once every use has been documented.

The imprest system is like refilling a car's fuel tank to full after every trip — you always know the tank's true starting capacity, and refilling exactly matches what was actually used.

How the imprest system works

StepWhat happens
1. Fix the float amountE.g., $100 is set as the petty cash fund's fixed level
2. Spend and recordEach purchase is documented with a receipt
3. Total the receiptsAt refill time, all receipts are added up
4. Top up to the fixed amountThe fund is replenished by exactly the amount spent

Why this matters to you

The imprest system makes petty cash easy to control precisely because the fund should always equal cash-on-hand plus receipts — if that total doesn't match the fixed float amount, an error or missing receipt is immediately obvious.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a $100 imprest petty cash fund has $65 cash remaining and $35 in receipts, confirm those two numbers add up to the original $100 float.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Imprest systemA method of topping petty cash back up to a fixed amount after each use
FloatThe fixed starting amount a petty cash fund is maintained at
Study tip: At refill time, always confirm that cash-on-hand plus total receipts equals the fixed float exactly — any mismatch should be investigated immediately, not simply adjusted away.

lessons.title: 4.6 Bank Statements
lessons.html:
Bank StatementsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Bank Statements

Bank Statements is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Your own records say the business has $2,000 in the bank. Is that figure something you should just trust completely, or should you check it against something else?

Bank Statements

In plain words

A bank statement is a report issued by the bank showing every transaction and the resulting balance in an account over a specific period.

A bank statement is like an independent referee's record of a game — even if you've been keeping your own score, the bank's own independent record is what actually confirms what really happened in the account.

What a bank statement shows

DetailPurpose
Opening and closing balanceThe account balance at the start and end of the period
DepositsMoney that went into the account
Withdrawals/chargesMoney that left the account, including bank fees
Transaction datesExactly when each transaction was processed by the bank

Why this matters to you

A bank statement is an independent, external confirmation of what actually happened in an account — comparing it against your own cashbook records is exactly what the next lesson, bank reconciliation, is built around.

🧪 Try it yourself: If you have access to a real or sample bank statement, identify its opening balance, one deposit, one withdrawal, and its closing balance.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Bank statementA bank-issued report showing all transactions and balances for an account
Bank chargeA fee the bank deducts from an account, shown on the statement
Study tip: Review your bank statement regularly, not just once a year — catching an unexpected charge or error early is always easier to resolve than discovering it months later.

lessons.title: 4.7 Bank Reconciliation
lessons.html:
Bank ReconciliationLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Bank Reconciliation

Bank Reconciliation is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Your cashbook says $2,000. The bank statement says $1,950. Both records were kept carefully. So which one is actually wrong?

Bank Reconciliation

In plain words

Bank reconciliation is the process of comparing your own cash records against the bank statement and explaining any differences between them.

Bank reconciliation is like comparing two people's separate notes from the same meeting — both might be accurate, just recorded at slightly different times or with slightly different details, and reconciling means explaining every difference clearly.

Common reasons for a difference

ReasonExplanation
Outstanding chequesA cheque you wrote hasn't been cashed by the recipient yet
Deposits in transitMoney you've recorded as deposited, but the bank hasn't processed yet
Bank chargesFees the bank deducted that you haven't recorded yet
ErrorsA mistake in either your records or the bank's

Why this matters to you

Regular bank reconciliation is one of the most important controls in all of bookkeeping — it catches bank fees you forgot to record, and just as importantly, it can catch fraud or errors before they grow into a much bigger problem.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using the example from the hook ($2,000 in your cashbook vs. $1,950 on the bank statement), suggest one possible reason for that $50 difference.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Bank reconciliationComparing your own records against the bank statement and explaining differences
Outstanding chequeA cheque that has been written and recorded but not yet cashed
Study tip: Reconcile your bank account monthly at minimum — the longer you wait, the more differences accumulate, and the harder it becomes to trace each one back to its actual cause.

A cheque that bounced due to insufficient funds

questions.explanation: Regular reconciliation helps catch discrepancies early, protecting the business from unnoticed errors or fraud.

lessons.title: 4.8 Common Reconciliation Errors
lessons.html:
Common Reconciliation ErrorsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Common Reconciliation Errors

Common Reconciliation Errors is the focus of this Cash and Bank Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to control cash, maintain cashbooks, and reconcile bank records.

cashbook

A record of cash and bank receipts and payments.

bank reconciliation

A comparison explaining differences between cashbook and bank statement balances.

imprest system

A petty-cash system that restores a fixed float after reimbursement.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You've reconciled your bank account, and the numbers still don't match. Are there a few usual suspects worth checking first, before assuming something serious is wrong?

Common Reconciliation Errors

In plain words

This lesson covers the most frequent reconciliation errors — mistakes bookkeepers repeatedly make — so you can check for them first when numbers don't match.

These common errors are like a mechanic's checklist of the most frequent, simple causes of a car problem — before assuming something is seriously wrong, it's worth ruling out the usual, simple suspects first.

Frequent reconciliation mistakes

MistakeHow to catch it
Transposed numbers (writing 45 instead of 54)Check if the difference is evenly divisible by 9
A transaction recorded twiceLook for duplicate entries of the same amount and date
A transaction missed entirelyCompare every bank statement line against your own records
Bank charges not yet recordedCheck the bank statement for any small deducted fees

Why this matters to you

Knowing these common patterns in advance turns reconciliation from an intimidating mystery into a systematic checklist — most real-world discrepancies trace back to exactly one of these few, well-known causes.

🧪 Try it yourself: If your reconciliation is off by an amount divisible by 9 (like 9, 18, 45, or 90), specifically check for a transposed-number error using the tip in the table above.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Transposed numbersAccidentally swapping two digits, like writing 54 instead of 45
Duplicate entryThe same transaction accidentally recorded more than once
Study tip: If a reconciliation difference is evenly divisible by 9, check for transposed digits first — it's a surprisingly reliable shortcut that catches one of the most common bookkeeping mistakes quickly.

lessons.title: 5.1 Sales Transactions
lessons.html:
Sales TransactionsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sales Transactions

Sales Transactions is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop sells a product for cash, and another sells the same product “on credit,” to be paid next month. Are these recorded the exact same way?

Sales Transactions

In plain words

A sales transaction is a completed sale of goods or services, recorded either as a cash sale (paid immediately) or a credit sale (payment owed later).

A cash sale is like buying something and paying on the spot; a credit sale is like a friend saying “I'll pay you back next week” — both are real sales, but the bookkeeping must reflect that one is already settled and the other is still owed.

Cash sale vs. credit sale

Cash saleCredit sale
PaymentReceived immediatelyOwed, to be paid later
Accounts affectedCash increases, Sales increasesAccounts Receivable increases, Sales increases

Why this matters to you

Recording a credit sale correctly (into Accounts Receivable, not Cash) is essential — recording it as if cash was already received would overstate how much actual cash the business has on hand.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write two simple journal entries: one for a $100 cash sale, and one for a $100 sale made on credit.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash saleA sale where payment is received immediately
Credit saleA sale where payment is owed and will be received later
Study tip: Always ask “has payment actually been received, or is it still owed?” before recording any sale — this single question determines whether Cash or Accounts Receivable is the correct account.

lessons.title: 5.2 Purchases Transactions
lessons.html:
Purchases TransactionsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Purchases Transactions

Purchases Transactions is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business buys supplies, paying immediately in one case and agreeing to pay the supplier next month in another. Does the bookkeeping distinguish between these two?

Purchases Transactions

In plain words

A purchases transaction is when a business acquires goods or services, recorded either as a cash purchase or a credit purchase, depending on when payment is made.

Just like sales, a purchase can be settled immediately (cash) or owed for later (credit) — the same underlying idea from sales transactions, just from the buyer's side instead of the seller's.

Cash purchase vs. credit purchase

Cash purchaseCredit purchase
PaymentMade immediatelyOwed, to be paid later
Accounts affectedCash decreases, an asset/expense increasesAccounts Payable increases, an asset/expense increases

Why this matters to you

Understanding purchases from the buyer's perspective (using Accounts Payable for credit purchases) is the direct mirror image of how sales are recorded from the seller's perspective — the same core logic, applied in the opposite direction.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write two journal entries: one for buying $80 of supplies with cash, and one for buying $80 of supplies on credit from a supplier.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash purchaseA purchase where payment is made immediately
Credit purchaseA purchase where payment is owed and will be made later
Study tip: Notice the pattern: Accounts Receivable tracks what customers owe YOU, while Accounts Payable tracks what YOU owe suppliers — mixing these two up is a common early bookkeeping mistake.

lessons.title: 5.3 Trade Discounts and Cash Discounts
lessons.html:
Trade Discounts and Cash DiscountsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Trade Discounts and Cash Discounts

Trade Discounts and Cash Discounts is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A supplier lists a product at $100, but offers 10% off for bulk orders, AND an extra 2% off if you pay within 10 days. Are both of these the same kind of discount?

Trade Discounts and Cash Discounts

In plain words

A trade discount is a reduction off the listed price (often for bulk buying), while a cash discount is a further reduction offered specifically for paying quickly.

A trade discount is like a bulk-buy price cut applied before you even start negotiating; a cash discount is like an extra “pay now and save” offer added on top, rewarding fast payment specifically.

Trade discount vs. cash discount

Trade discountCash discount
When appliedAt the time of sale, based on quantity or customer typeOnly if payment is made within a set time
Recorded in the books?No — the sale is recorded at the already-discounted priceYes — recorded separately as a discount allowed/received

Why this matters to you

This distinction matters directly for your bookkeeping: a trade discount is simply baked into the recorded sale price from the start, while a cash discount is its own separate transaction, recorded only if and when the early payment actually happens.

🧪 Try it yourself: A product listed at $200 gets a 10% trade discount, then a further 5% cash discount for paying within 7 days. Calculate the final amount actually paid.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Trade discountA price reduction off the listed price, often for bulk purchases
Cash discountA price reduction offered specifically for early or prompt payment
Study tip: Always apply the trade discount first to find the true selling price, and only then consider whether a further cash discount applies — the order genuinely matters for the final calculation.
