lessons.title: 5.4 Sales Returns and Purchase Returns
lessons.html:
Sales Returns and Purchase ReturnsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sales Returns and Purchase Returns

Sales Returns and Purchase Returns is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A customer returns a faulty product for a refund. Does that transaction just quietly disappear, or does it need its own proper record?

Sales Returns and Purchase Returns

In plain words

A sales return happens when a customer returns goods to your business, while a purchase return happens when your business returns goods to a supplier.

A sales return is like un-ringing a bell from the seller's side — the original sale still happened and should stay on record, but a clear, separate entry now shows that part of it was reversed.

Recording returns

Sales returnPurchase return
Who is returning goods?The customer, back to youYou, back to the supplier
EffectReduces your Sales and Accounts Receivable/CashReduces your Purchases and Accounts Payable/Cash

Why this matters to you

Recording returns separately (rather than just quietly deleting the original sale) keeps an honest, complete history — useful for spotting patterns like a specific product being returned unusually often.

🧪 Try it yourself: A customer buys $50 of goods on credit, then returns $20 worth as faulty. Write the two journal entries: the original credit sale, and the sales return.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Sales returnGoods returned by a customer back to the business
Purchase returnGoods the business returns back to a supplier
Study tip: Track returns by product or reason over time — a pattern of frequent returns for one specific item is valuable information about a quality or supplier problem worth investigating.

lessons.title: 5.5 Accounts Receivable
lessons.html:
Accounts ReceivableLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Accounts Receivable

Accounts Receivable is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Ten different customers currently owe your business money from credit sales. How do you keep track of exactly who owes what, and whether they've paid?

Accounts Receivable

In plain words

Accounts receivable is the total amount customers currently owe a business for goods or services already provided on credit.

Accounts receivable is like a shared notebook listing everyone who currently owes you money — not cash you have yet, but a clear, trackable promise of cash still coming.

Managing accounts receivable well

PracticeWhy it matters
Keep a subsidiary ledger per customerTracks exactly who owes what individually
Set clear payment termsE.g., “payment due within 30 days”
Follow up on overdue accountsPrevents debts from being forgotten or written off unnecessarily
Review the total regularlyConfirms it matches the general ledger control account

Why this matters to you

A business can look profitable on paper while quietly struggling for actual cash if too much money is tied up in accounts receivable that customers are slow to pay — managing this account well is directly connected to real cash flow health.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine three customers owing $100, $250, and $75. Calculate the total accounts receivable, and decide which customer you'd follow up with first and why.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Accounts receivableThe total amount customers currently owe a business for credit sales
Overdue accountA customer payment that is late compared to the agreed payment terms
Study tip: Follow up on overdue accounts promptly and consistently — the longer a debt goes unaddressed, the less likely it becomes that it will ever actually be collected.

lessons.title: 5.6 Accounts Payable
lessons.html:
Accounts PayableLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Accounts Payable

Accounts Payable is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Your business currently owes money to five different suppliers. How do you make sure none of those bills are accidentally missed or paid twice?

Accounts Payable

In plain words

Accounts payable is the total amount a business currently owes to its suppliers for goods or services received on credit.

Accounts payable is like a stack of bills waiting to be paid on their due dates — tracking them carefully ensures nothing is forgotten, and nothing is paid twice by mistake.

Managing accounts payable well

PracticeWhy it matters
Keep a subsidiary ledger per supplierTracks exactly what is owed to each one
Note each bill's due dateAvoids missing payments and damaging supplier relationships
Match invoices to paymentsConfirms each bill is paid exactly once, in full
Review the total regularlyConfirms it matches the general ledger control account

Why this matters to you

Managing accounts payable well protects a business's reputation and relationships with suppliers — consistently late or missed payments can damage trust and even cost a business favourable credit terms in the future.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine your business owes $150 to one supplier and $300 to another, both due in one week. Plan which to prioritise if cash is limited, and explain your reasoning.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Accounts payableThe total amount a business currently owes its suppliers
Due dateThe date by which a payment is expected to be made
Study tip: Always confirm an invoice against the actual goods or services received before paying it — paying an incorrect or duplicate invoice is a costly, avoidable mistake.

lessons.title: 5.7 Credit Control
lessons.html:
Credit ControlLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Credit Control

Credit Control is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business happily sells on credit to any customer who asks. Months later, several of them still haven't paid. Could this have been prevented?

Credit Control

In plain words

Credit control means managing who a business extends credit to, and how, in order to minimise the risk of not being paid.

Credit control is like a landlord checking references before renting an apartment — a little upfront caution and clear terms prevent a much bigger, harder-to-resolve problem later.

Elements of good credit control

ElementPurpose
Credit limitsA maximum amount a customer can owe at once
Clear payment termsE.g., “30 days from invoice date”
Credit checks for new customersAssessing a new customer's ability to pay before extending credit
Consistent follow-upChasing overdue payments promptly and professionally

Why this matters to you

Good credit control directly protects a business's cash flow — extending credit generously without any control feels friendly in the short term, but can quietly starve a business of the actual cash it needs to keep operating.

🧪 Try it yourself: Design a simple credit policy for an imaginary small business: what credit limit would you set for a new customer, and what payment terms would you require?

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Credit controlManaging who receives credit and how, to reduce the risk of non-payment
Credit limitThe maximum amount a customer is allowed to owe at one time
Study tip: Set clear credit limits and payment terms before extending credit to any customer, not after — establishing the rules upfront prevents most disputes and difficult conversations later.

lessons.title: 5.8 Bad Debts and Doubtful Debts
lessons.html:
Bad Debts and Doubtful DebtsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Bad Debts and Doubtful Debts

Bad Debts and Doubtful Debts is the focus of this Sales, Purchases & Trade lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record sales, purchases, discounts, returns, receivables, and payables.

accounts receivable

Amounts customers owe an organisation.

accounts payable

Amounts an organisation owes suppliers.

trade discount

A reduction from list price usually not recorded separately in the accounts.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A customer who owes your business $200 has vanished, and after a year of trying, you're now certain that money is never coming. Do you just keep listing it as an asset forever?

Bad Debts and Doubtful Debts

In plain words

A bad debt is a customer debt confirmed as uncollectible and written off, while a doubtful debt is one that might not be collected, so a provision is set aside just in case.

A doubtful debt is like setting aside a small “just in case” buffer when you're worried a friend might not repay you; a bad debt is finally accepting, with certainty, that the money is genuinely gone.

Bad debt vs. doubtful debt

Doubtful debtBad debt
CertaintyUncertain — might still be collectedCertain — confirmed as uncollectible
Accounting treatmentA provision (estimate) is set asideThe debt is fully written off

Why this matters to you

Recognising doubtful debts through a provision, rather than waiting until a debt is fully confirmed bad, gives a more honest, realistic picture of a business's true financial position at any given moment.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business believes 5% of its $2,000 total accounts receivable might not be collected, calculate the doubtful debt provision it should set aside.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Bad debtA customer debt confirmed as uncollectible and removed from the books
Provision for doubtful debtsAn estimated amount set aside for debts that might not be collected
Study tip: Review accounts receivable regularly for any debts that are becoming risky — recognising a doubtful debt early gives a more accurate, honest financial picture than waiting until it's fully confirmed lost.

lessons.title: 6.1 What Is Inventory?
lessons.html:
What Is Inventory?Lesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Inventory?

What Is Inventory? is the focus of this Inventory Management lesson. It develops the learner's ability to value, record, count, and protect inventory.

inventory

Goods held for sale or materials used in production.

FIFO

A valuation method assuming the earliest inventory is sold first.

cost of goods sold

The cost of inventory sold during a period.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop has shelves full of unsold products. Is that stock actually worth something on paper, or is it just physical stuff sitting there?

What Is Inventory?

In plain words

Inventory is the goods a business holds for the purpose of selling to customers, and it's recorded as an asset until it's actually sold.

Inventory is like ingredients sitting in a restaurant's kitchen — not yet turned into revenue, but genuinely valuable, and carefully counted, because it represents real money already spent, waiting to be converted into a sale.

Types of inventory

TypeExample
Raw materialsFabric a tailor hasn't yet sewn into clothing
Work-in-progressA half-finished piece of furniture
Finished goodsCompleted products ready to sell to customers

Why this matters to you

Inventory is treated as an asset on the balance sheet precisely because it holds real value — it only becomes an expense (Cost of Goods Sold) once it's actually sold, which is a distinction the next several lessons build directly on.

🧪 Try it yourself: List five items your household or a nearby shop currently has as “inventory” — goods held for future use or sale, not yet consumed or sold.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
InventoryGoods a business holds for the purpose of selling to customers
Finished goodsCompleted products that are ready to be sold
Study tip: Think of inventory as “money temporarily turned into goods” — it doesn't become a true expense until the moment it's actually sold to a customer.

lessons.title: 6.2 Inventory Valuation Methods
lessons.html:
Inventory Valuation MethodsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Inventory Valuation Methods

Inventory Valuation Methods is the focus of this Inventory Management lesson. It develops the learner's ability to value, record, count, and protect inventory.

inventory

Goods held for sale or materials used in production.

FIFO

A valuation method assuming the earliest inventory is sold first.

cost of goods sold

The cost of inventory sold during a period.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop buys the same product at three different prices over several months. When some of it sells, which price do you actually use to record the cost?

Inventory Valuation Methods

In plain words

Inventory valuation methods are the different rules a business can use to decide which cost to assign to inventory that was purchased at varying prices over time.

Imagine a jar where you keep adding coins of slightly different values over time — when you take some coins out, valuation methods are simply different rules for deciding WHICH specific coins you're considered to have taken.

Common valuation methods

MethodHow it works
FIFO (First-In, First-Out)Assumes the oldest inventory is sold first
Weighted AverageUses an average cost across all inventory purchased
LIFO (Last-In, First-Out)Assumes the newest inventory is sold first (less commonly used)

Why this matters to you

The valuation method chosen directly affects both the reported cost of goods sold and the value of remaining inventory on the balance sheet — meaning the same physical stock can show different profit figures depending on which method is used.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business bought inventory at $5, then $6, then $7 per unit, and now sells one unit, what cost would FIFO assign to that sale?

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Inventory valuationThe method used to assign cost to inventory purchased at different prices
FIFOFirst-In, First-Out — assuming the oldest inventory is sold first
Study tip: Once a business chooses a valuation method, it should apply it consistently — switching methods frequently makes it very difficult to compare financial performance accurately across different periods.

lessons.title: 6.3 FIFO and Weighted Average
lessons.html:
FIFO and Weighted AverageLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

FIFO and Weighted Average

FIFO and Weighted Average is the focus of this Inventory Management lesson. It develops the learner's ability to value, record, count, and protect inventory.

inventory

Goods held for sale or materials used in production.

FIFO

A valuation method assuming the earliest inventory is sold first.

cost of goods sold

The cost of inventory sold during a period.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You already know what FIFO and Weighted Average mean in theory. Could you actually calculate a real cost using each method, side by side?

FIFO and Weighted Average

In plain words

This lesson focuses on practically calculating inventory cost using both FIFO and Weighted Average, so you can confidently apply either method to real numbers.

Doing the actual calculation is like following a recipe rather than just reading about cooking — understanding the theory is a first step, but doing the maths yourself is what makes the method genuinely usable.

Worked example: 10 units bought at $4, then 10 units bought at $6

MethodCost assigned when 5 units are sold
FIFO5 units × $4 = $20 (uses the oldest, cheaper batch first)
Weighted AverageAverage cost = ($4+$6)/2 = $5; 5 units × $5 = $25

Why this matters to you

Practising this calculation with simple numbers now builds the confidence you'll need later when preparing real cost of goods sold figures for an actual business's financial statements.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using the same worked example numbers, calculate the cost assigned if 8 units (instead of 5) were sold, under both FIFO and Weighted Average.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cost per unitThe price assigned to a single unit of inventory
BatchA group of inventory units purchased together at the same price
Study tip: Practice this calculation with a few different simple number sets until it feels comfortable — this specific skill comes up constantly in real bookkeeping for any business that sells physical goods.

questions.explanation: The average of $4 and $6 across the two batches is $5 per unit.

questions.explanation: Each method makes a different assumption about which specific units' cost applies to a sale, producing different results.

lessons.title: 6.4 Stock Records and Stock Cards
lessons.html:
Stock Records and Stock CardsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Stock Records and Stock Cards

Stock Records and Stock Cards is the focus of this Inventory Management lesson. It develops the learner's ability to value, record, count, and protect inventory.

inventory

Goods held for sale or materials used in production.

FIFO

A valuation method assuming the earliest inventory is sold first.

cost of goods sold

The cost of inventory sold during a period.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop sells hundreds of different products. Without checking the physical shelf every single time, how would you know how many of one specific item are left?

Stock Records and Stock Cards

In plain words

Stock records and stock cards track the quantity and movement of each inventory item, showing what's been received, sold, and remains on hand.

A stock card is like a running scoreboard for one specific product — every time some comes in or goes out, the card updates, so the current total is always known without needing a physical recount.

What a stock card tracks

ColumnPurpose
DateWhen stock moved in or out
ReceivedQuantity added to stock
Issued/soldQuantity removed from stock
BalanceRunning total remaining

Why this matters to you

Accurate stock cards let a business know instantly which products are running low and need reordering, without waiting for a full, time-consuming physical stock count every time.

🧪 Try it yourself: Create a simple stock card for one product, recording: 20 units received, 8 sold, then 5 more received, keeping a running balance throughout.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Stock cardA record tracking one specific inventory item's movement and balance
Stock movementAny addition or removal of inventory, like a delivery or a sale
Study tip: Update stock cards at the moment stock actually moves (a delivery arrives, a sale happens) — waiting to update them later risks losing track of the true, current quantity.

lessons.title: 6.5 Physical Stock Counts
lessons.html:
Physical Stock CountsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Physical Stock Counts

Physical Stock Counts is the focus of this Inventory Management lesson. It develops the learner's ability to value, record, count, and protect inventory.

inventory

Goods held for sale or materials used in production.

FIFO

A valuation method assuming the earliest inventory is sold first.

cost of goods sold

The cost of inventory sold during a period.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Your stock records say you have 50 units of a product. Should you simply trust that number forever, or does someone need to actually go and count?

Physical Stock Counts

In plain words

A physical stock count means physically counting actual inventory on hand and comparing it to what the stock records say should be there.

A physical stock count is like a bank double-checking a vault's actual cash against its own records — even careful, well-kept records can drift from reality over time, and only a real, physical check confirms the truth.

Why physical counts matter

Reason records may be wrongHow a count catches it
Theft or lossPhysical count reveals fewer items than expected
Recording errorsA mismatch reveals a forgotten or duplicated entry
Damaged or spoiled goodsPhysically inspecting stock reveals items that should be written off

Why this matters to you

Regular physical stock counts — not just relying on stock cards — are one of the most effective ways to catch theft, damage, or recording errors before they grow into a much larger, harder-to-explain discrepancy.

🧪 Try it yourself: If your stock card says 50 units should be on hand, but a physical count finds only 45, describe two possible reasons for that 5-unit difference.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Physical stock countPhysically counting actual inventory and comparing it to recorded quantities
Stock discrepancyA difference between the physically counted quantity and the recorded quantity
Study tip: Schedule regular physical stock counts (monthly or quarterly, depending on the business), not just once a year — frequent counts catch problems while they're still small and easy to investigate.

lessons.title: 6.6 Cost of Goods Sold
lessons.html:
Cost of Goods SoldLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cost of Goods Sold

Cost of Goods Sold is the focus of this Inventory Management lesson. It develops the learner's ability to value, record, count, and protect inventory.

inventory

Goods held for sale or materials used in production.

FIFO

A valuation method assuming the earliest inventory is sold first.

cost of goods sold

The cost of inventory sold during a period.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop sells $500 worth of products in a month. Is that entire $500 profit, or does some of it just cover what the products themselves originally cost?

Cost of Goods Sold

In plain words

Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) is the direct cost of the inventory that was actually sold during a period, subtracted from sales revenue to calculate gross profit.

COGS is like the cost of ingredients in a meal you sell at a restaurant — the price a customer pays isn't pure profit; you must first subtract what those ingredients themselves cost you.

Calculating cost of goods sold

Formula elementExample
Opening inventory$1,000 worth of stock at the start of the period
+ Purchases$3,000 of new stock bought during the period
− Closing inventory$800 worth of stock remaining at the end
= Cost of Goods Sold$1,000 + $3,000 − $800 = $3,200

Why this matters to you

COGS is the direct link between inventory (an asset) and the income statement (an expense) — understanding this calculation is essential for correctly preparing the Gross Profit figure covered in the Financial Statements module ahead.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using the formula above, calculate COGS if opening inventory is $500, purchases during the period are $2,000, and closing inventory is $600.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)The direct cost of inventory actually sold during a period
Gross profitSales revenue minus the cost of goods sold
Study tip: Memorise the COGS formula (Opening Inventory + Purchases − Closing Inventory) thoroughly — it's one of the most frequently used calculations in the rest of this course.

lessons.title: 6.7 Inventory Control and Loss Prevention
lessons.html:
Inventory Control and Loss PreventionLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Inventory Control and Loss Prevention

Inventory Control and Loss Prevention is the focus of this Inventory Management lesson. It develops the learner's ability to value, record, count, and protect inventory.

inventory

Goods held for sale or materials used in production.

FIFO

A valuation method assuming the earliest inventory is sold first.

cost of goods sold

The cost of inventory sold during a period.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop's stock keeps mysteriously shrinking faster than sales alone would explain. Is that just bad luck, or a sign that something specific needs fixing?

Inventory Control and Loss Prevention

In plain words

Inventory control means the practices a business uses to protect its stock from theft, damage, and waste, keeping actual losses to a minimum.

Inventory control is like locking valuable items in a secure room instead of leaving them in an open hallway — the goods themselves haven't changed, but the level of protection around them has.

Key inventory control practices

PracticeWhy it helps
Secure storageLimits opportunities for theft
Limited accessFewer people handling stock reduces risk
Regular physical countsQuickly reveals unexplained losses
Clear reorder proceduresPrevents both running out and over-ordering

Why this matters to you

Strong inventory control directly protects a business's profit — unexplained stock loss (called “shrinkage”) is a quiet, ongoing cost that can seriously erode profit margins if left unaddressed for too long.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of one inventory control practice from the table above that a small shop you know could realistically start using, and explain why it would help.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Inventory controlPractices protecting stock from theft, damage, and waste
ShrinkageUnexplained inventory loss, often due to theft, damage, or error
Study tip: Combine several inventory control practices together (secure storage, limited access, regular counts) rather than relying on just one — layered protection is far more effective than any single measure alone.

lessons.title: 7.1 Payroll Basics
lessons.html:
Payroll BasicsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Payroll Basics

Payroll Basics is the focus of this Payroll and Staff Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to calculate payroll and maintain accurate, controlled staff records.

gross pay

Total earnings before deductions.

net pay

The amount paid after deductions.

statutory deduction

A legally required amount withheld from employee pay.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business has five employees. Is paying them simply a matter of handing over an agreed amount of cash each month?

Payroll Basics

In plain words

Payroll is the process of calculating, recording, and paying employee wages accurately and on time, including any required deductions.

Payroll is like a carefully checked recipe followed the same way every single time — small, repeated mistakes (a missed deduction, a wrong hourly rate) quietly compound into serious problems if the process isn't handled consistently.

Core parts of payroll

ElementWhat it covers
Gross pay calculationThe full amount earned before any deductions
DeductionsTaxes and other amounts subtracted from pay
Net payThe final amount the employee actually receives
Payroll recordsDocumentation of every payment made

Why this matters to you

Accurate, on-time payroll is one of the clearest ways a business builds trust with its employees — payroll mistakes, even unintentional ones, can seriously damage staff morale and trust in the organisation.

🧪 Try it yourself: List the names of five imaginary employees and their agreed monthly pay, as if you were about to begin processing payroll for them.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
PayrollThe process of calculating, recording, and paying employee wages
Gross payThe full amount an employee earns before any deductions
Study tip: Process payroll the same way, on the same schedule, every single pay period — consistency is what prevents the small errors that quietly damage employee trust over time.

lessons.title: 7.2 Gross Pay and Net Pay
lessons.html:
Gross Pay and Net PayLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Gross Pay and Net Pay

Gross Pay and Net Pay is the focus of this Payroll and Staff Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to calculate payroll and maintain accurate, controlled staff records.

gross pay

Total earnings before deductions.

net pay

The amount paid after deductions.

statutory deduction

A legally required amount withheld from employee pay.

🤔 Let's start with a question
An employee's contract says they earn $500 a month. Does $500 actually land in their bank account, or does something happen to that number first?

Gross Pay and Net Pay

In plain words

Gross pay is an employee's total earnings before deductions, while net pay is the actual amount they receive after taxes and other deductions are subtracted.

Gross pay is like a full basket of fruit before some is set aside for others; net pay is what's actually left in the basket for the employee to take home after those portions are removed.

From gross pay to net pay

StepExample
Gross pay$500
− Tax deduction− $50
− Other deductions (e.g. pension)− $20
= Net pay$430

Why this matters to you

Employees should always be able to clearly see the breakdown from gross to net pay — a payslip showing exactly what was deducted, and why, prevents confusion and builds trust in the payroll process.

🧪 Try it yourself: If an employee's gross pay is $600, with $60 tax and $15 other deductions, calculate their net pay.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Gross payTotal earnings before any deductions
Net payThe actual amount an employee receives after deductions
Study tip: Always clarify whether a stated salary is gross or net — this simple confusion can lead to serious misunderstandings during hiring negotiations and budgeting.

lessons.title: 7.3 Statutory Deductions
lessons.html:
Statutory DeductionsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Statutory Deductions

Statutory Deductions is the focus of this Payroll and Staff Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to calculate payroll and maintain accurate, controlled staff records.

gross pay

Total earnings before deductions.

net pay

The amount paid after deductions.

statutory deduction

A legally required amount withheld from employee pay.

🤔 Let's start with a question
An employer wants to deduct taxes from an employee's pay. Is that entirely up to the employer's own personal choice?

Statutory Deductions

In plain words

Statutory deductions are amounts an employer is legally required to withhold from an employee's pay, such as income tax and social security contributions.

Statutory deductions are like a toll booth an employer is legally required to collect on behalf of the government — the employer isn't choosing to take this money for themselves; they're required to collect and pass it along.

Common statutory deductions

DeductionPurpose
Income tax (PAYE)Tax on the employee's earnings, paid to the government
Social security contributionsFunds retirement, health, or welfare programs
Other legally required deductionsVary by country and specific regulations

Why this matters to you

Employers who fail to correctly withhold and remit statutory deductions can face serious legal and financial penalties — this is one area of payroll where following the exact legal requirements, not just convenience, genuinely matters.

🧪 Try it yourself: Research (or recall) one statutory deduction required in your own country and briefly explain its purpose.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Statutory deductionAn amount an employer is legally required to withhold from pay
PAYE (Pay As You Earn)A common system where income tax is deducted directly from wages
Study tip: Always confirm the exact statutory deduction rates and rules that apply in your own country before processing real payroll — these requirements can change and vary significantly by location.

lessons.html:
Payroll RecordsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Payroll Records

Payroll Records is the focus of this Payroll and Staff Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to calculate payroll and maintain accurate, controlled staff records.

gross pay

Total earnings before deductions.

net pay

The amount paid after deductions.

statutory deduction

A legally required amount withheld from employee pay.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A tax authority asks a business to prove exactly what it paid an employee eight months ago, and what was deducted. Could the business actually produce that proof?

Payroll Records

In plain words

Payroll records are the documented history of every employee payment, including gross pay, deductions, and net pay, kept for as long as legally required.

Payroll records are like a detailed, dated receipt book for every single payment made to every employee — without them, questions about past pay become impossible to answer with any real confidence.

What payroll records should include

DetailWhy it's needed
Employee name and IDIdentifies exactly who was paid
Pay periodThe specific time period the payment covers
Gross pay, deductions, net payThe full breakdown of the payment
Payment dateConfirms exactly when payment was made

Why this matters to you

Complete, accurate payroll records protect both the employer and employee — they resolve pay disputes quickly, support tax compliance, and provide the evidence needed if a payment is ever formally questioned.

🧪 Try it yourself: Design a simple payroll record template including all four details from the table above, for one imaginary employee's most recent pay period.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Payroll recordA documented history of an employee's pay, deductions, and payment date
Pay periodThe specific span of time a particular payment covers
Study tip: Keep payroll records organised and easily retrievable for at least as long as your country's laws require — losing these records can create serious problems during a tax audit or employee dispute.

lessons.title: 7.5 Employee Benefits
lessons.html:
Employee BenefitsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Employee Benefits

Employee Benefits is the focus of this Payroll and Staff Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to calculate payroll and maintain accurate, controlled staff records.

gross pay

Total earnings before deductions.

net pay

The amount paid after deductions.

statutory deduction

A legally required amount withheld from employee pay.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Two job offers pay the exact same salary. One also includes health insurance and paid leave. Are these two offers really equal in value?

Employee Benefits

In plain words

Employee benefits are additional forms of compensation beyond salary — like health insurance, paid leave, or a pension contribution — that add real value to an employee's total compensation.

Benefits are like the extra amenities that come with an apartment beyond just the rent price — a slightly higher rent with parking and security included can be a better overall deal than a cheaper apartment with nothing extra.

Common employee benefits

BenefitValue to the employee
Health insuranceCovers medical costs, reducing financial risk
Paid leaveTime off work without losing income
Pension contributionsBuilds savings for the employee's future
Training opportunitiesBuilds skills and career growth

Why this matters to you

From a bookkeeping perspective, benefits are a real cost to the business, just like salary, and should be properly recorded and budgeted for — not treated as an afterthought outside the normal payroll process.

🧪 Try it yourself: List two benefits (beyond salary) that would genuinely make a job offer more attractive to you personally, and explain why.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Employee benefitAdditional compensation beyond salary, like insurance or paid leave
Total compensationThe full value of pay plus benefits an employee receives
Study tip: When comparing job offers or planning a budget, always consider total compensation (salary plus benefits), not salary alone — it gives a far more accurate picture of real value.

lessons.title: 7.6 Payroll Taxes
lessons.html:
Payroll TaxesLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Payroll Taxes

Payroll Taxes is the focus of this Payroll and Staff Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to calculate payroll and maintain accurate, controlled staff records.

gross pay

Total earnings before deductions.

net pay

The amount paid after deductions.

statutory deduction

A legally required amount withheld from employee pay.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Beyond deducting tax from an employee's own pay, does the employer ALSO have to pay any tax themselves, just for having staff?

Payroll Taxes

In plain words

Payroll taxes are taxes related to employment that may be paid by the employee (through deductions), the employer directly, or both.

Payroll taxes are like a toll road with charges for both the passenger AND the vehicle owner — some payroll-related taxes come out of the employee's pay, while others are a separate, additional cost the employer must pay themselves.

Employee-paid vs. employer-paid payroll taxes

Employee-paidEmployer-paid
How it worksDeducted directly from the employee's gross payAn additional cost paid by the employer, on top of wages
ExampleIncome tax withheld from wagesEmployer's own social security contribution

Why this matters to you

Employer-paid payroll taxes are a real, additional cost of employing someone, beyond just their salary — understanding this helps a business accurately calculate the TRUE total cost of each employee, not just their visible wage.

🧪 Try it yourself: If an employee's salary is $500 and the employer must also separately pay a 5% employer social security contribution, calculate that additional employer cost.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Payroll taxA tax related to employment, paid by the employee, employer, or both
Employer contributionAn amount the employer pays in addition to an employee's wages
Study tip: When budgeting for a new hire, always calculate the FULL cost — salary plus any employer-paid payroll taxes and benefits — not just the advertised salary figure alone.

lessons.title: 7.7 Payroll Fraud Prevention
lessons.html:
Payroll Fraud PreventionLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Payroll Fraud Prevention

Payroll Fraud Prevention is the focus of this Payroll and Staff Records lesson. It develops the learner's ability to calculate payroll and maintain accurate, controlled staff records.

gross pay

Total earnings before deductions.

net pay

The amount paid after deductions.

statutory deduction

A legally required amount withheld from employee pay.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business discovers a “ghost employee” — someone being paid a salary who doesn't actually work there. How does something like that even happen?

Payroll Fraud Prevention

In plain words

Payroll fraud prevention means putting controls in place to stop dishonest manipulation of payroll, such as fake employees, inflated hours, or unauthorised pay changes.

Payroll fraud prevention is like having more than one person check an important document before it's finalised — a second set of eyes on payroll makes it far harder for a single dishonest person to quietly manipulate the system.

Common payroll fraud risks and controls

RiskPrevention
“Ghost employees” (fake staff on payroll)Regularly verify every employee actually exists and works there
Inflated hours or overtimeRequire supervisor approval of hours before payment
Unauthorised pay rate changesRequire a second approval for any pay rate change
One person controlling the whole payroll processSeparate who calculates, approves, and pays payroll

Why this matters to you

Payroll fraud is a genuine, common risk precisely because payroll often involves large, recurring payments trusted to relatively few people — the specific controls in this lesson exist because this exact type of fraud happens regularly in real organisations.

🧪 Try it yourself: Pick one payroll fraud risk from the table above and explain, in your own words, why the matching control actually helps prevent it.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Ghost employeeA fake or no-longer-employed person kept on payroll to divert pay fraudulently
Segregation of dutiesSeparating who calculates, approves, and pays payroll so no one person controls the whole process
Study tip: Never let one single person have complete, unchecked control over the entire payroll process — separating calculation, approval, and payment among different people is one of the strongest protections against payroll fraud.

lessons.title: 8.1 What Are Fixed Assets?
lessons.html:
What Are Fixed Assets?Lesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Are Fixed Assets?

What Are Fixed Assets? is the focus of this Fixed Assets and Depreciation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record fixed assets, depreciation, registers, and disposals.

fixed asset

A long-term resource used in operations rather than held for resale.

depreciation

Systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

carrying amount

Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business buys a delivery van it plans to use for the next ten years. Is that recorded the same way as buying $50 of office paper?

What Are Fixed Assets?

In plain words

Fixed assets are long-term items a business owns and uses over several years to help run its operations, rather than items bought to resell quickly.

A fixed asset is like a business's own tools and equipment — a carpenter's saw is used again and again for years, unlike the wood they buy to sell as finished furniture, which moves through quickly.

Examples of fixed assets

Fixed assetHow it's used
BuildingsOffice or shop space used for years
VehiclesDelivery or transport used repeatedly over time
Equipment and machineryTools used to produce goods or services
Furniture and fixturesDesks, shelving, and similar long-term items

Why this matters to you

Fixed assets are treated differently in bookkeeping from regular expenses precisely because their value and usefulness last for years — the next lesson (Capital vs Revenue Expenditure) explains exactly how to tell the two apart.

🧪 Try it yourself: List three fixed assets a small business you know (a shop, a farm, an office) would likely own and use for several years.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Fixed assetA long-term item a business owns and uses over several years
Long-term useAn item's benefit or usefulness lasting well beyond one accounting period
Study tip: Ask “will this item still be useful to the business next year, and the year after?” — if the answer is yes, it's very likely a fixed asset, not a regular expense.

lessons.title: 8.2 Capital vs Revenue Expenditure
lessons.html:
Capital vs Revenue ExpenditureLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Capital vs Revenue Expenditure

Capital vs Revenue Expenditure is the focus of this Fixed Assets and Depreciation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record fixed assets, depreciation, registers, and disposals.

fixed asset

A long-term resource used in operations rather than held for resale.

depreciation

Systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

carrying amount

Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business spends $5,000 buying a new delivery van, and also spends $50 on fuel for it that same week. Are both of these recorded the exact same way?

Capital vs Revenue Expenditure

In plain words

Capital expenditure buys or improves a long-term fixed asset, while revenue expenditure covers regular, everyday costs of running the business.

Capital expenditure is like buying the car itself; revenue expenditure is like paying for the fuel to run it — one is a long-term investment, the other is an ongoing, repeated cost of use.

Telling the two apart

Capital expenditureRevenue expenditure
ExampleBuying a delivery vanBuying fuel for the van
Accounting treatmentRecorded as an asset, spread over its useful lifeRecorded immediately as an expense
Benefit periodSeveral yearsThe current period only

Why this matters to you

Getting this classification right matters directly for accurate financial statements — treating a capital purchase as a regular expense would make that period's profit look artificially low, while the opposite mistake would make an asset's value look inflated.

🧪 Try it yourself: Classify these as capital or revenue expenditure: buying a new office building, repainting an existing office wall, and buying a new computer for the office.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Capital expenditureSpending that buys or improves a long-term fixed asset
Revenue expenditureSpending on regular, ongoing costs of running the business
Study tip: Ask “does this spending create or improve a long-term asset, or does it just cover a regular cost of today's operations?” — the answer tells you immediately whether it's capital or revenue expenditure.

lessons.title: 8.3 Depreciation Methods
lessons.html:
Depreciation MethodsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Depreciation Methods

Depreciation Methods is the focus of this Fixed Assets and Depreciation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record fixed assets, depreciation, registers, and disposals.

fixed asset

A long-term resource used in operations rather than held for resale.

depreciation

Systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

carrying amount

Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business buys equipment for $10,000. Five years later, is that equipment on the books still worth the exact same $10,000?

Depreciation Methods

In plain words

Depreciation is the process of spreading a fixed asset's cost over its useful life, reflecting that the asset gradually loses value as it's used.

Depreciation is like tracking a car's declining value each year you own it — the car still runs, but everyone recognises it's worth less than when it was brand new, and depreciation is simply recording that gradual loss.

Why depreciation matters

ReasonExplanation
Matches cost to benefitSpreads an asset's cost across the years it's actually used
Reflects true valueShows a more realistic asset value over time, not the original price forever
Affects profitDepreciation is recorded as an expense, reducing reported profit

Why this matters to you

Depreciation connects directly to the matching concept covered later in this course — the cost of a fixed asset is deliberately spread across the years it actually helps generate income, rather than being expensed all at once in the year of purchase.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a fixed asset you own personally (like a phone or bicycle). Estimate roughly how many years it will remain useful, and describe how its value has already changed since you got it.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
DepreciationSpreading a fixed asset's cost over its useful life
Useful lifeThe estimated period of time an asset will remain usable
Study tip: Estimate a reasonable useful life for every fixed asset when it's first purchased — this estimate is what the depreciation methods in the next two lessons will actually be calculated from.

lessons.title: 8.4 Straight-Line Depreciation
lessons.html:
Straight-Line DepreciationLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Straight-Line Depreciation

Straight-Line Depreciation is the focus of this Fixed Assets and Depreciation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record fixed assets, depreciation, registers, and disposals.

fixed asset

A long-term resource used in operations rather than held for resale.

depreciation

Systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

carrying amount

Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business buys equipment for $10,000, expects it to last 5 years, and estimates it will be worth $0 at the end. Is there a simple way to spread that cost evenly?

Straight-Line Depreciation

In plain words

Straight-line depreciation spreads an asset's cost evenly across its useful life, resulting in the exact same depreciation expense every single year.

Straight-line depreciation is like slicing a cake into equal-sized pieces — regardless of the total number of years, each year gets exactly the same-sized “slice” of the total cost.

Calculating straight-line depreciation

Formula elementExample
Cost of asset$10,000
− Estimated residual value− $0
÷ Useful life (years)÷ 5 years
= Annual depreciation$2,000 per year

Why this matters to you

Straight-line is the most widely used depreciation method specifically because of its simplicity — it's easy to calculate, easy to explain, and produces a predictable, consistent expense every year.

🧪 Try it yourself: Calculate the annual straight-line depreciation for equipment costing $8,000, with an estimated residual value of $500, over a 5-year useful life.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Straight-line depreciationA method spreading an asset's cost evenly across its useful life
Residual valueThe estimated value an asset will still have at the end of its useful life
Study tip: Memorise the straight-line formula thoroughly — (Cost − Residual Value) ÷ Useful Life — since it's the depreciation method you'll use most often in practice.

questions.explanation: Its simplicity and predictability make straight-line depreciation the most widely used method.

lessons.title: 8.5 Reducing Balance Depreciation
lessons.html:
Reducing Balance DepreciationLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Reducing Balance Depreciation

Reducing Balance Depreciation is the focus of this Fixed Assets and Depreciation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record fixed assets, depreciation, registers, and disposals.

fixed asset

A long-term resource used in operations rather than held for resale.

depreciation

Systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

carrying amount

Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A brand-new car loses much more of its value in year one than it does in year five. Does straight-line depreciation actually reflect that pattern?

Reducing Balance Depreciation

In plain words

Reducing balance depreciation applies a fixed percentage to an asset's remaining (not original) value each year, resulting in higher depreciation in earlier years and lower amounts later.

Reducing balance is like calculating interest on a shrinking loan balance — the percentage rate stays the same, but since it's applied to a smaller and smaller remaining amount each year, the actual depreciation amount shrinks over time too.

Calculating reducing balance depreciation

YearCalculationDepreciation
Year 120% of $10,000$2,000 (remaining value: $8,000)
Year 220% of $8,000$1,600 (remaining value: $6,400)
Year 320% of $6,400$1,280 (remaining value: $5,120)

Why this matters to you

Reducing balance depreciation suits assets (like vehicles or computers) that genuinely do lose more value early on — choosing between this method and straight-line should reflect how the specific asset actually behaves in the real world.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using a 25% reducing balance rate on a $4,000 asset, calculate the depreciation expense for Year 1 and Year 2.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Reducing balance depreciationA method applying a fixed percentage to an asset's remaining value each year
Remaining valueAn asset's value after subtracting depreciation already charged
Study tip: Choose reducing balance depreciation specifically for assets that genuinely lose value fastest when new (like vehicles or technology) — using it for assets that don't behave this way can misrepresent their real value.

lessons.title: 8.6 Asset Registers
lessons.html:
Asset RegistersLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Asset Registers

Asset Registers is the focus of this Fixed Assets and Depreciation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record fixed assets, depreciation, registers, and disposals.

fixed asset

A long-term resource used in operations rather than held for resale.

depreciation

Systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

carrying amount

Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business owns dozens of fixed assets — computers, furniture, vehicles. Without a single organised list, how would anyone track what's owned, its value, and its location?

Asset Registers

In plain words

An asset register is a detailed record listing every fixed asset a business owns, including its cost, depreciation, current value, and location.

An asset register is like a detailed inventory list for a museum's entire collection — not just what's owned, but where each piece is, what it's worth, and its full history, all organised in one place.

What an asset register tracks

DetailPurpose
Description and asset IDIdentifies exactly which asset this is
Purchase date and costRecords when and how much was paid
Depreciation method and rateShows how its value is being reduced over time
Current locationConfirms where the asset actually is

Why this matters to you

A well-maintained asset register supports accurate financial statements, makes physical asset verification far easier, and helps prevent assets from being lost, misplaced, or quietly disposed of without anyone noticing.

🧪 Try it yourself: Create a simple asset register entry for one fixed asset (like a computer), including all four details from the table above.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Asset registerA detailed record listing every fixed asset a business owns
Asset IDA unique identifier assigned to track a specific asset
Study tip: Update your asset register immediately whenever an asset is bought, moved, or disposed of — an outdated register quickly becomes far less useful for tracking what a business actually owns.

lessons.title: 8.7 Disposal of Fixed Assets
lessons.html:
Disposal of Fixed AssetsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Disposal of Fixed Assets

Disposal of Fixed Assets is the focus of this Fixed Assets and Depreciation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to record fixed assets, depreciation, registers, and disposals.

fixed asset

A long-term resource used in operations rather than held for resale.

depreciation

Systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.

carrying amount

Asset cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business sells an old delivery van it no longer needs. Does that transaction simply remove the van from the books, with nothing else to consider?

Disposal of Fixed Assets

In plain words

Disposal of fixed assets means removing a fixed asset from the books when it's sold, scrapped, or retired, and recording any resulting profit or loss.

Disposing of an asset is like finally selling an old car — you compare what you sell it for against what it was still recorded as being worth on your own books, and the difference is either a gain or a loss.

Calculating a gain or loss on disposal

ScenarioCalculationResult
Asset's book value is $1,000; sold for $1,200$1,200 − $1,000$200 gain
Asset's book value is $1,000; sold for $700$700 − $1,000$300 loss

Why this matters to you

Recording asset disposals correctly matters because the resulting gain or loss actually affects the business's reported profit for that period — an asset sold well above its book value genuinely improves that period's results, and vice versa.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a piece of equipment has a book value of $2,000 and is sold for $2,500, calculate the gain or loss on disposal.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Book valueAn asset's current recorded value after depreciation, before disposal
Gain/loss on disposalThe difference between an asset's sale price and its book value
Study tip: Always calculate an asset's current book value carefully before disposal — comparing the actual sale price against this figure is what tells you whether the disposal resulted in a genuine gain or loss.

lessons.title: 9.1 Purpose of Financial Statements
lessons.html:
Purpose of Financial StatementsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Purpose of Financial Statements

Purpose of Financial Statements is the focus of this Financial Statements I: Income Statement lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare and interpret an accurate income statement.

revenue

Income earned from ordinary activities.

gross profit

Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold.

net profit

The remaining profit after all relevant expenses.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You've now recorded transactions, journals, ledgers, cash, inventory, and payroll. What's actually the POINT of turning all of that into a few summary reports?

Purpose of Financial Statements

In plain words

Financial statements are formal reports summarising a business's financial performance and position, built specifically to help people understand and make decisions.

Financial statements are like a translated summary of a long, detailed novel — all the detail from months of individual transactions gets condensed into a clear, readable story anyone can actually understand quickly.

The main financial statements

StatementWhat it shows
Income statementProfit or loss over a period
Balance sheetWhat the business owns, owes, and is worth at one point in time
Cash flow statementHow cash moved in and out during a period

Why this matters to you

Everything you've learned so far in this course — journals, ledgers, trial balances — exists specifically to produce these final, readable reports; they are the actual destination of the entire accounting cycle.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of one specific question (like “did we make a profit?” or “what do we own?”) and match it to which financial statement would actually answer it.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Financial statementA formal report summarising financial performance or position
Financial positionWhat a business owns, owes, and is worth at a specific point in time
Study tip: As you learn to build each financial statement in this module, keep asking “what real question does this actually answer?” — it keeps the purpose behind the numbers clear.

lessons.title: 9.2 The Income Statement
lessons.html:
The Income StatementLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Income Statement

The Income Statement is the focus of this Financial Statements I: Income Statement lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare and interpret an accurate income statement.

revenue

Income earned from ordinary activities.

gross profit

Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold.

net profit

The remaining profit after all relevant expenses.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business earned $10,000 in sales this month, and spent $7,000 running the business. Is there one clear report that shows this whole story at once?

The Income Statement

In plain words

The income statement (also called a profit and loss statement) summarises a business's income and expenses over a period, showing whether it made a profit or a loss.

An income statement is like a scorecard for a specific game — it doesn't describe the whole team's history, just this one period's specific result: did income beat expenses, or not?

Basic structure of an income statement

SectionExample
Income (revenue)$10,000 in sales
− Expenses− $7,000 in costs
= Net profit (or loss)$3,000 net profit

Why this matters to you

The income statement answers one of the most fundamental questions any business owner asks: “did we actually make money this period?” — everything else in this statement exists to build toward that one clear answer.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business earned $15,000 in income and had $11,000 in total expenses this month, calculate its net profit or loss.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Income statementA report showing income and expenses over a period, and the resulting profit or loss
Net profitThe amount remaining after all expenses are subtracted from income
Study tip: Always check whether an income statement covers a month, a quarter, or a year — the specific time period matters just as much as the actual numbers themselves.

lessons.title: 9.3 Gross Profit and Net Profit
lessons.html:
Gross Profit and Net ProfitLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Gross Profit and Net Profit

Gross Profit and Net Profit is the focus of this Financial Statements I: Income Statement lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare and interpret an accurate income statement.

revenue

Income earned from ordinary activities.

gross profit

Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold.

net profit

The remaining profit after all relevant expenses.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business earns $10,000 in sales. Its cost of goods sold is $4,000, and its other expenses (rent, wages) total $3,000. Is “profit” here just one single number?

Gross Profit and Net Profit

In plain words

Gross profit is sales minus the cost of goods sold, while net profit is what remains after ALL expenses (including operating costs) are subtracted.

Gross profit is like the money left after buying the ingredients for food you sell; net profit is what's left after ALSO paying for the stall rent, staff, and every other cost of actually running the business.

From sales to net profit

StepAmount
Sales$10,000
− Cost of goods sold− $4,000
= Gross profit$6,000
− Other operating expenses− $3,000
= Net profit$3,000

Why this matters to you

Distinguishing gross profit from net profit reveals different problems: weak gross profit suggests a pricing or product-cost issue, while strong gross profit but weak net profit points instead to high operating expenses.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using the numbers in the table above, confirm the gross profit and net profit calculations yourself, step by step.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Gross profitSales minus the cost of goods sold
Operating expensesThe regular costs of running a business, like rent and wages
Study tip: When a business seems to be selling well but still isn't very profitable, check gross profit AND net profit separately — the gap between them usually reveals exactly where the real problem lies.

lessons.title: 9.4 Operating Expenses
lessons.html:
Operating ExpensesLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Operating Expenses

Operating Expenses is the focus of this Financial Statements I: Income Statement lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare and interpret an accurate income statement.

revenue

Income earned from ordinary activities.

gross profit

Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold.

net profit

The remaining profit after all relevant expenses.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop's rent, staff wages, and electricity bill all need to be paid every month, regardless of how many sales happen. What category do these all belong to?

Operating Expenses

In plain words

Operating expenses are the regular, ongoing costs of running a business, separate from the direct cost of the goods or services it sells.

Operating expenses are like the background costs of keeping a restaurant's doors open — rent, staff, electricity — that must be paid whether the restaurant is busy or nearly empty that day.

Common operating expenses

ExpenseExample
RentMonthly payment for business premises
Wages and salariesStaff pay, separate from cost of goods
UtilitiesElectricity, water, internet
Administrative costsOffice supplies, insurance, professional fees

Why this matters to you

Operating expenses are what actually gets subtracted from gross profit to reach net profit — controlling these costs carefully is one of the most direct, practical ways a business owner can genuinely improve overall profitability.

🧪 Try it yourself: List three operating expenses a small shop would likely have every single month, regardless of how many sales it makes.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Operating expenseA regular, ongoing cost of running a business
Fixed costA cost that stays roughly the same regardless of sales volume, like rent
Study tip: Review operating expenses regularly for ones that could realistically be reduced — unlike cost of goods sold, many operating expenses (subscriptions, unused services) can often be cut without affecting sales at all.

lessons.title: 9.5 Accruals and Prepayments
lessons.html:
Accruals and PrepaymentsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Accruals and Prepayments

Accruals and Prepayments is the focus of this Financial Statements I: Income Statement lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare and interpret an accurate income statement.

revenue

Income earned from ordinary activities.

gross profit

Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold.

net profit

The remaining profit after all relevant expenses.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business used electricity all through December, but the bill doesn't actually arrive until January. Which month's expense does that cost really belong to?

Accruals and Prepayments

In plain words

An accrual records an expense or income in the period it actually relates to, even if cash hasn't yet changed hands. A prepayment is the opposite — paying in advance for something not yet used.

Accruals and prepayments are like adjusting a shared bill fairly by actual usage — even if payment happens at a different time, the accounting should still reflect the period the cost or benefit truly belongs to.

Accruals vs. prepayments

AccrualPrepayment
ExampleDecember's electricity bill, paid in JanuaryPaying a full year's insurance in advance
Timing mismatchExpense happens before cash is paidCash is paid before the expense is actually used up

Why this matters to you

Accruals and prepayments are what make financial statements genuinely accurate for the period they cover — without these adjustments, expenses would be recorded in whichever month cash happened to move, not the month they actually relate to.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business pays $1,200 for a full year of insurance in January, calculate how much of that cost should be recognised as an expense for just the month of January.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
AccrualRecording an expense or income in the period it relates to, regardless of cash timing
PrepaymentPaying in advance for something not yet used or received
Study tip: Whenever cash is paid or received at a different time than when the related expense or income actually occurs, ask “which period does this REALLY belong to?” — that question is the heart of accruals and prepayments.

lessons.title: 9.6 Matching Concept
lessons.html:
Matching ConceptLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Matching Concept

Matching Concept is the focus of this Financial Statements I: Income Statement lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare and interpret an accurate income statement.

revenue

Income earned from ordinary activities.

gross profit

Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold.

net profit

The remaining profit after all relevant expenses.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business earns income in March from a product whose materials were actually bought back in January. Should that cost be recorded as a January expense or a March one?

Matching Concept

In plain words

The matching concept says expenses should be recorded in the same period as the income they helped generate, not simply whenever the cash was paid.

The matching concept is like properly crediting ingredients to the meal they were actually used in — even if you bought those ingredients weeks earlier, their cost belongs to the specific meal (and its resulting income) they helped create.

Applying the matching concept

SituationHow matching applies
Materials bought in January, product sold in MarchThe materials' cost is matched to March, when the related sale occurs
A December electricity bill paid in JanuaryThe expense is matched to December, when the electricity was actually used

Why this matters to you

The matching concept is the underlying reason accruals, prepayments, and even cost of goods sold work the way they do — nearly every timing adjustment covered in this module exists specifically to properly apply this one core principle.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of one transaction where the timing of a cash payment and the timing of the related income or benefit are actually different, and explain how the matching concept would treat it.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Matching conceptRecording expenses in the same period as the income they helped generate
Timing mismatchWhen cash payment and the related expense or income occur in different periods
Study tip: Whenever you're deciding which period an expense belongs to, ask “which period's income did this expense actually help generate?” — that question captures the entire matching concept in one sentence.

lessons.title: 9.7 Preparing a Simple Income Statement
lessons.html:
Preparing a Simple Income StatementLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Preparing a Simple Income Statement

Preparing a Simple Income Statement is the focus of this Financial Statements I: Income Statement lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare and interpret an accurate income statement.

revenue

Income earned from ordinary activities.

gross profit

Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold.

net profit

The remaining profit after all relevant expenses.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You understand every individual piece — income, cost of goods sold, gross profit, expenses, net profit. Can you now actually put them together into one real report?

Preparing a Simple Income Statement

In plain words

This lesson walks through preparing a complete, simple income statement from start to finish, combining every concept from this module into one finished document.

Building a full income statement is like assembling a complete recipe after already practising each individual cooking technique separately — now you combine them all, in the right order, into one finished result.

Building the statement step by step

LineAmount
Sales$20,000
− Cost of goods sold− $8,000
= Gross profit$12,000
− Operating expenses (rent, wages, utilities)− $7,000
= Net profit$5,000

Why this matters to you

Being able to build a complete income statement confidently, from raw figures to a finished report, is one of the most immediately useful and employable bookkeeping skills covered in this entire course.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using your own imagined numbers, build a complete income statement following the exact same five-line structure shown in the table above.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Income statement structureThe standard sequence: sales, cost of goods sold, gross profit, expenses, net profit
Finished reportA complete, properly formatted financial statement ready to be read by others
Study tip: Practice building complete income statements with several different sets of numbers until the five-line structure feels automatic — this exact structure will reappear constantly in your future bookkeeping work.

modules.title: Module 10: Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet

lessons.title: 10.1 The Balance Sheet
lessons.html:
The Balance SheetLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Balance Sheet

The Balance Sheet is the focus of this Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare a balanced statement of financial position.

asset

A resource controlled by an organisation that is expected to provide benefit.

liability

A present obligation expected to require settlement.

equity

The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

🤔 Let's start with a question
The income statement shows a period's profit. But if someone asks “what is this business actually worth RIGHT NOW,” does the income statement answer that?

The Balance Sheet

In plain words

The balance sheet is a snapshot, at one specific point in time, of everything a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and its owner's stake (equity).

If the income statement is a video showing a period of activity, the balance sheet is a single photograph — capturing exactly what the business looks like financially at one specific, frozen moment.

The basic structure of a balance sheet

SectionExample
AssetsCash, inventory, equipment — what the business owns
LiabilitiesLoans, unpaid bills — what the business owes
EquityOwner's investment plus retained profit

Why this matters to you

The balance sheet is directly built from the accounting equation covered back in Module 1 (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) — everything in this module is really just that same simple equation, expanded into full, real-world detail.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a business you know and list one thing it owns (an asset) and one thing it owes (a liability), just to start thinking in balance sheet terms.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Balance sheetA snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity at one point in time
SnapshotA view of something at one specific, frozen moment, rather than over a period
Study tip: Remember the key difference: the income statement covers a PERIOD (like a month), while the balance sheet captures a single POINT in time — mixing these up is a common early misunderstanding.

lessons.title: 10.2 Assets, Liabilities and Equity in Detail
lessons.html:
Assets, Liabilities and Equity in DetailLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Assets, Liabilities and Equity in Detail

Assets, Liabilities and Equity in Detail is the focus of this Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare a balanced statement of financial position.

asset

A resource controlled by an organisation that is expected to provide benefit.

liability

A present obligation expected to require settlement.

equity

The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You know the basic accounting equation. But within “assets” alone, are cash, inventory, and a building all really treated exactly the same way?

Assets, Liabilities and Equity in Detail

In plain words

Going deeper than the basic equation, assets, liabilities, and equity each break down into more specific categories that reveal more detail about a business's financial position.

This deeper detail is like moving from a simple map showing just “city” and “countryside” to a detailed map showing individual streets and landmarks — same overall picture, but with far more useful specific information.

Detailed categories

CategoryIncludes
AssetsCash, inventory, equipment, buildings, accounts receivable
LiabilitiesLoans, accounts payable, unpaid taxes, accrued expenses
EquityOwner's capital invested, retained earnings, drawings

Why this matters to you

Understanding these detailed categories is essential for correctly building a real balance sheet — the next few lessons in this module (current vs non-current, working capital) all depend on being able to correctly classify items within these broader groups.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take five items (cash, a bank loan, a building, unpaid supplier invoices, owner's investment) and correctly sort each one into Assets, Liabilities, or Equity.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Accrued expenseAn expense that has been incurred but not yet paid, classified as a liability
Retained earningsProfit kept in the business rather than paid out to the owner
Study tip: When unsure how to classify an item, ask the basic questions first: “does the business own this?” (asset), “does it owe this?” (liability), or “is this the owner's own stake?” (equity).

Current vs Non-Current ItemsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Current vs Non-Current Items

Current vs Non-Current Items is the focus of this Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare a balanced statement of financial position.

asset

A resource controlled by an organisation that is expected to provide benefit.

liability

A present obligation expected to require settlement.

equity

The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business has cash it will use this week, and a building it will use for the next twenty years. Should both really sit in the exact same category?

Current vs Non-Current Items

In plain words

Current assets and liabilities are expected to be used, collected, or paid within one year, while non-current items are expected to last, or be owed, for longer than a year.

Current items are like groceries you'll use up this week; non-current items are like a large freezer you'll keep and use for years — both are genuinely valuable, but on very different timescales.

Current vs. non-current examples

CurrentNon-current
AssetsCash, inventory, accounts receivableBuildings, vehicles, long-term equipment
LiabilitiesAccounts payable, a short-term loan due this yearA mortgage or long-term loan due after a year

Why this matters to you

This distinction matters directly for assessing a business's short-term financial health — comparing current assets to current liabilities (covered next in Working Capital) reveals whether a business can comfortably cover what it owes in the near term.

🧪 Try it yourself: Sort these five items into current or non-current: cash, a 20-year building loan, inventory, a supplier invoice due next month, and company vehicles used for years.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
CurrentExpected to be used, collected, or paid within one year
Non-currentExpected to last, or be owed, for longer than one year
Study tip: Ask “will this be used up, collected, or paid within the next twelve months?” — a clear yes means current; a clear no means non-current.
