lessons.title: 10.4 Owner's Equity and Drawings
lessons.html:
Owner's Equity and DrawingsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Owner's Equity and Drawings

Owner's Equity and Drawings is the focus of this Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare a balanced statement of financial position.

asset

A resource controlled by an organisation that is expected to provide benefit.

liability

A present obligation expected to require settlement.

equity

The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

🤔 Let's start with a question
An owner takes $200 out of the business for personal use. Is that recorded as a business expense, the same as paying rent?

Owner's Equity and Drawings

In plain words

Owner's equity is the owner's total stake in the business, and drawings are amounts the owner personally withdraws for their own use, reducing that equity.

Drawings are like a business partner taking their own personal share out of a shared pot — it's not a cost of running the business itself, it's simply the owner reducing their own remaining stake in it.

How drawings affect equity

ElementEffect on equity
Owner's initial investmentIncreases equity
Retained profitIncreases equity
Drawings (personal withdrawals)Decreases equity

Why this matters to you

Drawings must be recorded separately from business expenses — mixing personal withdrawals in with genuine business costs like rent or wages would make the business's true operating expenses, and its real profitability, look inaccurate.

🧪 Try it yourself: If an owner invested $5,000, the business earned $2,000 in retained profit, and the owner withdrew $800 in drawings, calculate the owner's final equity.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
DrawingsAmounts an owner personally withdraws from the business for their own use
Owner's equityThe owner's total stake in the business
Study tip: Always record drawings in their own separate account, distinct from business expenses — this keeps the business's true operating costs and the owner's personal withdrawals clearly, honestly separated.

lessons.title: 10.5 Working Capital
lessons.html:
Working CapitalLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Working Capital

Working Capital is the focus of this Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare a balanced statement of financial position.

asset

A resource controlled by an organisation that is expected to provide benefit.

liability

A present obligation expected to require settlement.

equity

The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business owns valuable buildings and equipment worth millions. But could it still run out of cash to pay this month's bills?

Working Capital

In plain words

Working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities, showing whether a business has enough short-term resources to cover its near-term obligations.

Working capital is like checking whether you have enough cash and quickly-sellable items on hand to cover this month's bills — regardless of how valuable your house or car might be, those don't help pay a bill due next week.

Calculating working capital

ElementAmount
Current assets$8,000
− Current liabilities− $5,000
= Working capital$3,000

Why this matters to you

Positive working capital suggests a business can comfortably meet its short-term obligations, while negative working capital is a warning sign — even a business with valuable long-term assets can face serious trouble if it can't cover what's due soon.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business has $12,000 in current assets and $9,500 in current liabilities, calculate its working capital and state whether that's a healthy sign.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Working capitalCurrent assets minus current liabilities
Short-term obligationA debt or payment due within the next year
Study tip: Check working capital regularly, not just overall asset value — a business can look wealthy on paper while still genuinely struggling to pay its bills if its working capital is weak or negative.

lessons.title: 10.6 Preparing a Simple Balance Sheet
lessons.html:
Preparing a Simple Balance SheetLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Preparing a Simple Balance Sheet

Preparing a Simple Balance Sheet is the focus of this Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare a balanced statement of financial position.

asset

A resource controlled by an organisation that is expected to provide benefit.

liability

A present obligation expected to require settlement.

equity

The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You understand assets, liabilities, and equity individually. Can you now actually assemble them into one real, complete balance sheet?

Preparing a Simple Balance Sheet

In plain words

This lesson walks through preparing a complete, simple balance sheet, combining assets, liabilities, and equity into one properly organised financial statement.

Assembling a full balance sheet is like putting together a completed jigsaw puzzle after already sorting all the individual pieces by category — now everything comes together into one clear, complete picture.

Building the statement step by step

SectionAmount
Current assets (cash, inventory)$8,000
Non-current assets (equipment)$12,000
Total assets$20,000
Total liabilities (loans, payables)$9,000
Total equity (owner's stake)$11,000

Why this matters to you

Confirming that total assets ($20,000) equals total liabilities plus equity ($9,000 + $11,000 = $20,000) is the final, essential check — if these don't match, something earlier in your figures needs to be reviewed and corrected.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using your own imagined figures, build a complete simple balance sheet, and confirm that total assets equal total liabilities plus equity.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Total assetsThe complete sum of everything a business owns
Balance sheet checkConfirming total assets equal total liabilities plus equity
Study tip: Always perform the final check — total assets must equal total liabilities plus equity — before considering any balance sheet finished; an unbalanced sheet means an error exists somewhere in your figures.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Preparing a Simple Balance Sheet
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes above, then answer these to confirm you understood Preparing a Simple Balance Sheet.

lessons.title: 10.7 Linking the Income Statement and Balance Sheet
lessons.html:
Linking the Income Statement and Balance SheetLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Linking the Income Statement and Balance Sheet

Linking the Income Statement and Balance Sheet is the focus of this Financial Statements II: Balance Sheet lesson. It develops the learner's ability to prepare a balanced statement of financial position.

asset

A resource controlled by an organisation that is expected to provide benefit.

liability

A present obligation expected to require settlement.

equity

The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business's income statement shows $3,000 net profit this year. Does that profit figure just disappear once the report is finished, or does it actually go somewhere?

Linking the Income Statement and Balance Sheet

In plain words

The income statement and balance sheet are directly connected: a period's net profit flows into the balance sheet, increasing the owner's retained earnings within equity.

These two statements are like two connected rooms in the same house — profit earned in one room (the income statement) doesn't just vanish; it flows through and adds to what's stored in the next room (equity on the balance sheet).

How profit connects the two statements

StatementWhat happens
Income statementShows $3,000 net profit for the year
Balance sheetRetained earnings within equity increases by that same $3,000

Why this matters to you

Understanding this connection is what makes financial statements feel like one coherent, connected system rather than three separate, unrelated documents — a business's performance (income statement) directly shapes its financial position (balance sheet).

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business's equity was $10,000 at the start of the year, and it earned $2,500 net profit with no drawings, calculate its equity at the end of the year.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Retained earningsAccumulated profit kept in the business, part of owner's equity
Connected statementsFinancial statements that flow into and affect one another
Study tip: Whenever you review a set of financial statements, trace how the net profit or loss figure flows from the income statement into the balance sheet's equity section — it's the thread connecting the whole system together.

lessons.title: 11.1 Understanding Cash Flow
lessons.html:
Understanding Cash FlowLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Understanding Cash Flow

Understanding Cash Flow is the focus of this Cash Flow and Budgeting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to analyse cash movement, prepare budgets, and manage shortages.

cash flow

Movement of cash and cash equivalents into and out of an organisation.

cash budget

A forecast of expected cash receipts, payments, and balances.

variance

The difference between an actual amount and a planned amount.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business's income statement shows a healthy $5,000 profit this month. Yet it still can't pay its rent on time. How is that even possible?

Understanding Cash Flow

In plain words

Cash flow is the actual movement of cash into and out of a business, which can differ significantly from the profit shown on the income statement.

Profit is like the score of a game, while cash flow is like your actual physical energy during it — you can be “winning” on paper while still running out of the real, immediate resource (cash) you need to keep playing.

Why profit and cash flow can differ

ReasonEffect
Credit salesProfit is recorded, but the cash hasn't been collected yet
Buying inventory or assetsCash goes out, even though it doesn't appear as an expense immediately
Loan repaymentsReduces cash, but doesn't appear on the income statement at all

Why this matters to you

Many genuinely profitable businesses have failed simply because they ran out of actual cash — understanding that profit and cash flow are two different things entirely is one of the most important lessons in all of practical bookkeeping.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of one reason (from the table above or your own idea) why a business could be profitable on paper but still short of actual cash.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash flowThe actual movement of cash into and out of a business
Cash flow problemA shortage of actual usable cash, even while a business appears profitable
Study tip: Never assume a profitable business is automatically safe — always check its actual cash position separately, since profit and cash flow can tell two very different stories.

lessons.title: 11.2 The Cash Flow Statement
lessons.html:
The Cash Flow StatementLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

The Cash Flow Statement

The Cash Flow Statement is the focus of this Cash Flow and Budgeting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to analyse cash movement, prepare budgets, and manage shortages.

cash flow

Movement of cash and cash equivalents into and out of an organisation.

cash budget

A forecast of expected cash receipts, payments, and balances.

variance

The difference between an actual amount and a planned amount.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You now understand WHY profit and cash can differ. Is there an actual report that lays out exactly where a business's cash came from and went?

The Cash Flow Statement

In plain words

The cash flow statement shows all the cash a business received and paid out during a period, organised into clear categories.

A cash flow statement is like a detailed bank statement summary specifically for the business, but organised by WHY the cash moved (day-to-day operations, investments, financing), not just listed randomly in date order.

The three sections of a cash flow statement

SectionExample
Operating activitiesCash from sales, cash paid for expenses
Investing activitiesCash used to buy equipment, cash from selling an asset
Financing activitiesCash from a loan, cash used to repay a loan or pay the owner

Why this matters to you

The cash flow statement completes the picture alongside the income statement and balance sheet — together, these three statements show a business's performance, its position, and exactly how its cash actually moved, from three different angles.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take three cash transactions you can imagine for a small business, and sort each one into operating, investing, or financing activities.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash flow statementA report showing cash received and paid, organised by operating, investing, and financing activities
Operating activitiesCash flows related to a business's normal, day-to-day operations
Study tip: When reviewing a cash flow statement, pay closest attention to the operating activities section — it reveals whether the core, everyday business itself is generating or consuming cash, separate from one-off investments or loans.

lessons.title: 11.3 Operating, Investing and Financing Activities
lessons.html:
Operating, Investing and Financing ActivitiesLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Operating, Investing and Financing Activities

Operating, Investing and Financing Activities is the focus of this Cash Flow and Budgeting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to analyse cash movement, prepare budgets, and manage shortages.

cash flow

Movement of cash and cash equivalents into and out of an organisation.

cash budget

A forecast of expected cash receipts, payments, and balances.

variance

The difference between an actual amount and a planned amount.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business receives cash from a sale, from selling old equipment, and from a new bank loan — all in the same week. Are these three cash inflows really the same TYPE of activity?

Operating, Investing and Financing Activities

In plain words

This lesson looks more closely at how to classify cash movements correctly into operating, investing, or financing activities.

Think of these three categories like three different reasons money might move through your own personal life: your regular job income (operating), selling an old asset like a car (investing), or borrowing/repaying a loan (financing) — each is a genuinely different TYPE of cash movement.

Classifying common cash movements

Cash movementCategory
Cash received from a customer saleOperating
Cash paid for wages or rentOperating
Cash paid to buy a vehicleInvesting
Cash received from a bank loanFinancing
Cash paid to the owner as drawingsFinancing

Why this matters to you

Correctly classifying cash movements reveals genuinely different insights — strong operating cash flow shows the core business itself is healthy, while relying heavily on financing cash flow (loans) to stay afloat can be a warning sign worth investigating.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take five real or imagined cash movements from a business and classify each one correctly into operating, investing, or financing.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Investing activitiesCash flows related to buying or selling long-term assets
Financing activitiesCash flows related to loans, owner investment, or owner withdrawals
Study tip: When classifying a cash movement, ask “is this from normal daily operations, buying/selling a long-term asset, or a loan/owner transaction?” — that single question sorts it into the correct category almost every time.

lessons.title: 11.4 Preparing a Cash Budget
lessons.html:
Preparing a Cash BudgetLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Preparing a Cash Budget

Preparing a Cash Budget is the focus of this Cash Flow and Budgeting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to analyse cash movement, prepare budgets, and manage shortages.

cash flow

Movement of cash and cash equivalents into and out of an organisation.

cash budget

A forecast of expected cash receipts, payments, and balances.

variance

The difference between an actual amount and a planned amount.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You want to know, in advance, whether your business will have enough cash to cover next month's expenses. Can you actually plan that ahead of time?

Preparing a Cash Budget

In plain words

A cash budget is a forward-looking plan estimating expected cash inflows and outflows for a future period, helping identify potential shortfalls before they happen.

A cash budget is like planning a road trip's fuel stops in advance — rather than discovering you're low on fuel unexpectedly, you plan ahead based on the distance and your tank's capacity.

Building a simple cash budget

LineExample
Opening cash balance$1,000
+ Expected cash inflows+ $5,000 (expected sales)
− Expected cash outflows− $4,500 (rent, wages, supplies)
= Closing cash balance$1,500

Why this matters to you

A cash budget lets a business owner see a potential cash shortage coming weeks in advance — giving them real time to react (delay a purchase, chase an overdue payment) instead of discovering the problem only once it's already a genuine crisis.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using your own estimated numbers, build a simple one-month cash budget following the four-line structure in the table above.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash budgetA forward-looking plan estimating future cash inflows and outflows
Cash shortfallA predicted or actual situation where cash outflows exceed available cash
Study tip: Build a rolling cash budget (updated regularly, looking a few months ahead) rather than a single static one — a business's real cash position changes constantly, and the budget should be kept current to stay useful.

lessons.title: 11.5 Variance Analysis
lessons.html:
Variance AnalysisLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Variance Analysis

Variance Analysis is the focus of this Cash Flow and Budgeting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to analyse cash movement, prepare budgets, and manage shortages.

cash flow

Movement of cash and cash equivalents into and out of an organisation.

cash budget

A forecast of expected cash receipts, payments, and balances.

variance

The difference between an actual amount and a planned amount.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Your cash budget predicted $5,000 in sales this month. Actual sales came in at $4,200. Is that gap something worth actually investigating?

Variance Analysis

In plain words

Variance analysis compares budgeted (planned) figures against actual results, to understand and explain any differences.

Variance analysis is like comparing your planned travel budget against what you actually spent on a trip — the real value isn't just noticing a difference exists, but understanding exactly WHY it happened.

Understanding a variance

StepQuestion to ask
1. Calculate the varianceActual minus budgeted figure
2. Determine directionIs actual higher or lower than planned?
3. Investigate the causeWhy did the actual result differ from the plan?
4. Decide on actionDoes anything need to change going forward?

Why this matters to you

Regular variance analysis turns a budget from a one-time guess into an ongoing learning tool — each variance, properly investigated, teaches something that makes the NEXT budget more accurate and realistic.

🧪 Try it yourself: If budgeted sales were $5,000 and actual sales were $4,200, calculate the variance and suggest one possible reason for it.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
VarianceThe difference between a budgeted figure and the actual result
Favourable/unfavourable varianceWhether a variance represents a better or worse outcome than planned
Study tip: Treat every significant variance as a learning opportunity, not just a number to record — understanding why a budget was wrong is exactly what makes each future budget more accurate.

lessons.title: 11.6 Managing Cash Shortfalls
lessons.html:
Managing Cash ShortfallsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Managing Cash Shortfalls

Managing Cash Shortfalls is the focus of this Cash Flow and Budgeting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to analyse cash movement, prepare budgets, and manage shortages.

cash flow

Movement of cash and cash equivalents into and out of an organisation.

cash budget

A forecast of expected cash receipts, payments, and balances.

variance

The difference between an actual amount and a planned amount.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Your cash budget predicts you'll be $500 short next month. Panicking aside, what are your actual, practical options?

Managing Cash Shortfalls

In plain words

Managing cash shortfalls means having practical strategies ready for when a business anticipates or experiences a temporary lack of available cash.

Managing a shortfall is like navigating a temporary dip in personal income — there are several sensible options (delaying a purchase, asking for extra time, drawing on savings) rather than just panicking or ignoring the problem.

Practical strategies for a cash shortfall

StrategyHow it helps
Chase overdue customer paymentsBrings expected cash in sooner
Delay non-urgent purchasesReduces cash going out temporarily
Negotiate supplier payment termsBuys extra time before payments are due
Arrange short-term financingProvides a temporary cash buffer if genuinely needed

Why this matters to you

Having these strategies ready BEFORE a shortfall actually happens — because your cash budget warned you in advance — is exactly why the earlier lessons on cash budgeting and variance analysis matter so directly in real, practical terms.

🧪 Try it yourself: Using the $500 shortfall example from the hook, choose one strategy from the table above and explain specifically how you'd apply it.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cash shortfallA situation where a business has less cash available than it needs
Negotiate payment termsArranging with a supplier for more time to pay an amount owed
Study tip: Address a predicted cash shortfall as early as possible, using the mildest effective strategy first (like chasing a late payment) before resorting to more serious options like emergency borrowing.

lessons.title: 11.7 Forecasting for Small Organizations
lessons.html:
Forecasting for Small OrganizationsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Forecasting for Small Organizations

Forecasting for Small Organizations is the focus of this Cash Flow and Budgeting lesson. It develops the learner's ability to analyse cash movement, prepare budgets, and manage shortages.

cash flow

Movement of cash and cash equivalents into and out of an organisation.

cash budget

A forecast of expected cash receipts, payments, and balances.

variance

The difference between an actual amount and a planned amount.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A church, a small NGO, and a shop all want to plan ahead financially. Does “forecasting” really only apply to big, complex businesses?

Forecasting for Small Organizations

In plain words

Financial forecasting means estimating future income and expenses, and it's just as valuable — and just as achievable — for small organisations as it is for large ones.

Forecasting for a small organisation is like a household planning next month's budget based on past spending patterns — it doesn't require complex tools, just a realistic look at what's actually likely to happen next.

Simple forecasting for small organisations

StepExample
1. Review past patternsLook at the last 3-6 months of income and expenses
2. Adjust for known changesA new donor, a rent increase, a seasonal slow period
3. Estimate conservativelySlightly underestimate income, slightly overestimate expenses
4. Review and update regularlyCompare against actual results and adjust the next forecast

Why this matters to you

Even a very small church, NGO, or shop benefits enormously from basic forecasting — it doesn't require expensive software or a finance degree, just the willingness to look honestly at past patterns and plan a reasonable step ahead.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a small organisation you're familiar with (your own church, a family business, a school club) and sketch a simple, one-line forecast for its income next month.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
ForecastingEstimating future income and expenses based on available information
Conservative estimateA cautious estimate that slightly underestimates income or overestimates costs
Study tip: Start forecasting with just the last few months of your own real numbers — even a very simple, honest estimate based on real past patterns is far more useful than no forecast at all.

lessons.title: 12.1 What Is Cost Accounting?
lessons.html:
What Is Cost Accounting?Lesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Cost Accounting?

What Is Cost Accounting? is the focus of this Cost Accounting Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to classify costs, calculate break-even, and support pricing decisions.

fixed cost

A cost that remains stable within a relevant activity range.

variable cost

A cost changing with activity or output.

break-even point

The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A factory knows its total expenses for the month. But does it actually know how much it costs to produce just ONE single unit of its product?

What Is Cost Accounting?

In plain words

Cost accounting is a branch of accounting focused specifically on tracking, analysing, and controlling the costs of producing goods or services.

If financial accounting is like a company's report card for outsiders, cost accounting is like a coach's detailed practice notes — used internally to understand exactly where effort (and cost) is going, so decisions can be made about producing more efficiently.

What cost accounting focuses on

Focus areaExample question it answers
Cost per unitHow much does it cost to make one item?
Cost behaviourWhich costs change with production volume, and which don't?
Pricing decisionsWhat price covers our costs and earns a profit?
EfficiencyWhere can costs be reduced without harming quality?

Why this matters to you

Cost accounting is primarily used internally by managers making operational decisions, unlike financial accounting's reports, which are built mainly for external users like banks and investors — this distinction connects directly back to the “branches of accounting” lesson from Module 1.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a product or service a small business you know sells, and list two individual costs (materials, labour, packaging) that go into making just ONE unit of it.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cost accountingA branch of accounting focused on tracking and controlling production costs
Cost per unitThe cost of producing a single item or delivering one service
Study tip: As you move through this module, keep asking “how does this specific cost information actually help someone make a better business decision?” — that's the whole practical purpose of cost accounting.

lessons.title: 12.2 Fixed and Variable Costs
lessons.html:
Fixed and Variable CostsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Fixed and Variable Costs

Fixed and Variable Costs is the focus of this Cost Accounting Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to classify costs, calculate break-even, and support pricing decisions.

fixed cost

A cost that remains stable within a relevant activity range.

variable cost

A cost changing with activity or output.

break-even point

The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A bakery pays the same rent whether it sells 10 loaves or 1,000 loaves this month. But its flour costs clearly depend on how much it actually bakes. Are these the same TYPE of cost?

Fixed and Variable Costs

In plain words

A fixed cost stays the same regardless of production volume, while a variable cost changes directly with how much is produced or sold.

Fixed costs are like a gym membership fee — the same whether you go once or thirty times a month; variable costs are like the actual food you eat — the more you consume, the more it costs, scaling directly with use.

Fixed vs. variable cost examples

Fixed costsVariable costs
RentRaw materials
InsuranceDirect labour paid per unit produced
Manager's salaryPackaging materials

Why this matters to you

Understanding which of a business's costs are fixed versus variable is the essential foundation for break-even analysis, covered in the very next lesson — you cannot calculate a break-even point without first separating these two cost types clearly.

🧪 Try it yourself: Classify these costs as fixed or variable for a small bakery: monthly rent, flour used per loaf, and the owner's fixed monthly salary.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Fixed costA cost that stays the same regardless of production volume
Variable costA cost that changes directly with production or sales volume
Study tip: For every cost a business has, ask “would this cost change at all if we produced zero units this month?” — if no, it's fixed; if yes, it's variable.

lessons.title: 12.3 Direct and Indirect Costs
lessons.html:
Direct and Indirect CostsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Direct and Indirect Costs

Direct and Indirect Costs is the focus of this Cost Accounting Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to classify costs, calculate break-even, and support pricing decisions.

fixed cost

A cost that remains stable within a relevant activity range.

variable cost

A cost changing with activity or output.

break-even point

The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A furniture maker buys wood for a specific chair, and also pays for the general electricity bill lighting the whole workshop. Are both of these costs tied to that ONE chair in the same way?

Direct and Indirect Costs

In plain words

A direct cost can be traced specifically to one product or service, while an indirect cost supports the business more broadly and can't be tied to just one item.

A direct cost is like the specific wood used in one particular chair — you can point to exactly which product it belongs to; an indirect cost is like the workshop's electricity bill — it supports everything being made, not just one specific item.

Direct vs. indirect cost examples

Direct costsIndirect costs
Wood used for a specific chairWorkshop electricity bill
Fabric used for one dressRent for the whole workshop
Labour paid specifically to build one itemA supervisor's general salary

Why this matters to you

Understanding this distinction matters for accurately pricing individual products — a price based only on direct costs, while ignoring indirect costs entirely, can make a product look more profitable than it truly is once ALL its real costs are considered.

🧪 Try it yourself: For a small business you know (a tailor, a bakery, a carpenter), identify one direct cost and one indirect cost involved in making their product.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Direct costA cost that can be traced specifically to one product or service
Indirect costA cost supporting the business broadly, not traceable to just one item
Study tip: When pricing any product, make sure to account for a fair share of indirect costs too, not just the obvious direct materials and labour — otherwise your true cost, and true profit margin, will be understated.

lessons.title: 12.4 Break-even Analysis
lessons.html:
Break-even AnalysisLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Break-even Analysis

Break-even Analysis is the focus of this Cost Accounting Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to classify costs, calculate break-even, and support pricing decisions.

fixed cost

A cost that remains stable within a relevant activity range.

variable cost

A cost changing with activity or output.

break-even point

The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A small bakery wants to know exactly how many loaves it must sell each month just to stop losing money. Is there an actual calculation for that?

Break-even Analysis

In plain words

Break-even analysis calculates the exact sales volume at which total revenue equals total costs — the point where a business is neither making a profit nor a loss.

Break-even is like figuring out exactly how many tickets a small concert must sell just to cover the cost of renting the hall — sell fewer, and you lose money; sell more, and every extra ticket becomes genuine profit.

Calculating the break-even point

Formula elementExample
Fixed costs$2,000 per month
Selling price per unit$10
Variable cost per unit$6
Break-even units$2,000 ÷ ($10 − $6) = 500 units

Why this matters to you

Knowing the exact break-even point turns a vague goal like “sell more” into a precise, motivating target — anything sold beyond that specific number of units is genuine profit, giving a business owner a clear, meaningful benchmark.

🧪 Try it yourself: If fixed costs are $3,000, selling price is $15 per unit, and variable cost is $9 per unit, calculate the break-even point in units.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Break-even pointThe sales volume where total revenue exactly equals total costs
Contribution marginSelling price minus variable cost per unit
Study tip: Recalculate your break-even point whenever fixed costs, prices, or variable costs change significantly — an outdated break-even figure can quietly mislead important pricing and sales decisions.

lessons.title: 12.5 Contribution Margin
lessons.html:
Contribution MarginLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Contribution Margin

Contribution Margin is the focus of this Cost Accounting Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to classify costs, calculate break-even, and support pricing decisions.

fixed cost

A cost that remains stable within a relevant activity range.

variable cost

A cost changing with activity or output.

break-even point

The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A product sells for $10 and costs $6 in variable costs to make. Does that leftover $4 immediately count as pure profit?

Contribution Margin

In plain words

Contribution margin is the amount remaining from each sale after variable costs are covered, which first goes toward covering fixed costs, and only becomes profit once fixed costs are fully covered.

Contribution margin is like the money left after paying for ingredients at a food stall — that leftover amount first needs to cover the stall's daily rental fee (fixed cost) before any of it can actually be called profit.

Understanding contribution margin

StageWhat happens
Each unit soldContributes $4 (selling price $10 − variable cost $6)
Early salesContribution goes toward covering fixed costs
Once fixed costs are fully coveredEvery further unit's contribution becomes pure profit

Why this matters to you

Contribution margin is the exact figure used in the break-even formula from the previous lesson — understanding what it actually represents (not just how to calculate it) makes break-even analysis feel like a logical calculation, not just a memorised formula.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a product sells for $20 with $12 in variable costs, calculate its contribution margin per unit, and explain in your own words what that $8 actually represents.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Contribution marginThe amount remaining from a sale after variable costs, before fixed costs are covered
Profit thresholdThe point at which fixed costs are fully covered and further contribution becomes profit
Study tip: Calculate your product's contribution margin early in any pricing decision — a low or negative contribution margin is a serious warning sign that the price may not be sustainable, regardless of how many units are sold.

lessons.title: 12.6 Costing for Pricing Decisions
lessons.html:
Costing for Pricing DecisionsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Costing for Pricing Decisions

Costing for Pricing Decisions is the focus of this Cost Accounting Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to classify costs, calculate break-even, and support pricing decisions.

fixed cost

A cost that remains stable within a relevant activity range.

variable cost

A cost changing with activity or output.

break-even point

The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You know your product's exact direct and indirect costs. Does that information alone tell you what price to actually charge?

Costing for Pricing Decisions

In plain words

Costing for pricing decisions means using accurate cost information — direct, indirect, fixed, and variable — as one key input into setting a price that covers costs and earns a reasonable profit.

Costing informs pricing the way knowing a recipe's true ingredient cost informs a restaurant's menu price — you still consider what customers will pay and what competitors charge, but you never price below what it genuinely costs you to make.

How cost information supports pricing

Cost insightPricing implication
Full cost per unit (direct + a fair share of indirect)Sets the minimum price to avoid a loss
Contribution margin at different price pointsShows how profit changes if price is adjusted
Break-even volume at a given priceReveals whether that sales volume is realistically achievable

Why this matters to you

Cost accounting doesn't set a price by itself — it tells you the true floor below which you'd be losing money, while market research and competitor pricing (covered in the broader Entrepreneurship/Marketing courses) inform how much ABOVE that floor you can realistically charge.

🧪 Try it yourself: For a product you know the approximate cost of, calculate its full cost per unit and decide on a price that would give at least a 20% profit margin above that cost.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Cost-based pricingSetting a price using cost information as a key input
Profit marginThe percentage of a selling price that represents profit above cost
Study tip: Always know your true full cost per unit before setting any price — even the most attractive-sounding price is a mistake if it doesn't at least cover what the product genuinely costs to make.

lessons.title: 12.7 Budgetary Control
lessons.html:
Budgetary ControlLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Budgetary Control

Budgetary Control is the focus of this Cost Accounting Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to classify costs, calculate break-even, and support pricing decisions.

fixed cost

A cost that remains stable within a relevant activity range.

variable cost

A cost changing with activity or output.

break-even point

The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A department was given a budget of $10,000 for the year. Does anyone actually check, throughout the year, whether it's staying within that limit?

Budgetary Control

In plain words

Budgetary control means actively monitoring actual spending against a budget throughout the year, not just creating the budget once and setting it aside.

Budgetary control is like checking your fuel gauge regularly during a long trip, not just estimating fuel needs once at the very start — regular checks let you react to a problem while there's still time to do something about it.

Elements of budgetary control

ElementPurpose
Regular comparison reportsActual spending versus budgeted spending, checked monthly or quarterly
Variance investigationUnderstanding why actual spending differs from the budget
Corrective actionAdjusting spending or the budget itself based on what's found
AccountabilitySomeone specific is responsible for staying within budget

Why this matters to you

Budgetary control connects directly back to variance analysis from the Cash Flow and Budgeting module — the real value of any budget comes not from writing it, but from actively checking actual results against it throughout the period.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a budget you might set for yourself (like monthly spending money) and describe how you would actually check your real spending against it partway through the month.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Budgetary controlActively monitoring actual spending against a budget throughout a period
AccountabilityA specific person or team being responsible for staying within budget
Study tip: Set a specific, regular schedule (like monthly) for comparing actual results against any budget — a budget that's never actually checked provides no more real value than no budget at all.

lessons.title: 13.1 Introduction to Taxation
lessons.html:
Introduction to TaxationLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to Taxation

Introduction to Taxation is the focus of this Taxation Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to maintain tax records and understand basic filing responsibilities.

tax

A compulsory payment imposed by government.

withholding tax

Tax deducted at source before payment reaches the recipient.

tax return

A formal statement reporting taxable activity to an authority.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business earns good profit this year. Does all of that profit actually belong entirely to the owner, with nothing else to consider?

Introduction to Taxation

In plain words

Taxation is the legally required system through which businesses and individuals contribute a portion of their income or activity to government revenue.

Taxation is like every household in a neighbourhood contributing toward a shared service, like street lighting or a community well — everyone benefits from public services, and taxes are the shared, required way of funding them.

Why taxation matters for bookkeeping

ReasonExplanation
Legal requirementBusinesses are legally obligated to pay correctly and on time
Depends on accurate recordsTax calculations rely entirely on the bookkeeping records covered throughout this course
Real financial consequencesErrors or late payments can lead to penalties and interest charges

Why this matters to you

Every single topic covered earlier in this course — recording transactions, financial statements, cost tracking — ultimately supports accurate tax calculation and filing, making taxation a natural, practical destination for everything learned so far.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of one reason why a government might need tax revenue from businesses and individuals, based on public services you personally rely on.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
TaxationThe legally required system through which income or activity is taxed to fund government revenue
Tax complianceMeeting all legal requirements for correctly calculating and paying tax
Study tip: Think of good bookkeeping as your best protection during tax season — accurate, complete records throughout the year make tax calculation straightforward, rather than a stressful scramble.

lessons.title: 13.2 Types of Taxes Businesses Pay
lessons.html:
Types of Taxes Businesses PayLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Types of Taxes Businesses Pay

Types of Taxes Businesses Pay is the focus of this Taxation Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to maintain tax records and understand basic filing responsibilities.

tax

A compulsory payment imposed by government.

withholding tax

Tax deducted at source before payment reaches the recipient.

tax return

A formal statement reporting taxable activity to an authority.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business pays tax on its profit at year-end. Is that really the ONLY kind of tax a typical business deals with throughout the year?

Types of Taxes Businesses Pay

In plain words

Businesses typically encounter several types of taxes — including income tax, sales tax, and payroll-related taxes — each with its own rules and purpose.

Different tax types are like different tolls on different roads a business travels — one toll applies to profit earned, another to sales made, another to employees paid — each collected for a different reason, at a different point.

Common types of business taxes

Tax typeWhat it's based on
Income taxThe business's profit for the year
Sales tax / GST / VATSales made to customers
Payroll taxesEmployee wages (covered earlier in Module 7)
Property taxLand or buildings the business owns

Why this matters to you

Recognising which type of tax applies to which activity helps a business plan realistically — sales tax, for example, is generally collected from customers throughout the year, while income tax is typically settled based on the full year's final profit.

🧪 Try it yourself: For a small business you know, identify which of the tax types in the table above it most likely has to deal with.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means

Study tip: Research exactly which types of taxes apply to your own specific business and location — tax types and rates vary significantly by country, and assuming incorrectly can lead to real compliance problems.

lessons.title: 13.3 Income Tax Basics
lessons.html:
Income Tax BasicsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Income Tax Basics

Income Tax Basics is the focus of this Taxation Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to maintain tax records and understand basic filing responsibilities.

tax

A compulsory payment imposed by government.

withholding tax

Tax deducted at source before payment reaches the recipient.

tax return

A formal statement reporting taxable activity to an authority.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business earned $50,000 in profit this year. Does the government tax that entire amount, or just a portion of it?

Income Tax Basics

In plain words

Income tax is a tax calculated on a business's (or individual's) taxable income, which is often profit after allowable deductions, not simply total revenue.

Income tax is like paying a percentage of your net winnings after a game, not your total bets placed — it's calculated on what you actually kept as profit, after legitimate costs are already subtracted.

How income tax is generally calculated

StepExample
Total revenue$80,000
− Allowable business expenses− $50,000
= Taxable income$30,000
× Tax rate (example 25%)$30,000 × 25% = $7,500 tax owed

Why this matters to you

Income tax is calculated on taxable income, not total revenue — this is exactly why accurate income statements (built earlier in this course) matter so directly; the income statement's net profit figure is the very starting point for this tax calculation.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business has $40,000 in taxable income and a 20% income tax rate, calculate the income tax owed.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Taxable incomeIncome remaining after allowable deductions, on which tax is actually calculated
Tax rateThe percentage applied to taxable income to calculate tax owed
Study tip: Keep clear, complete records of every allowable business expense throughout the year — these deductions directly reduce taxable income, and disorganised records risk missing deductions a business is legitimately entitled to.

lessons.title: 13.4 Sales Tax and GST/VAT Concepts
lessons.html:
Sales Tax and GST/VAT ConceptsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sales Tax and GST/VAT Concepts

Sales Tax and GST/VAT Concepts is the focus of this Taxation Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to maintain tax records and understand basic filing responsibilities.

tax

A compulsory payment imposed by government.

withholding tax

Tax deducted at source before payment reaches the recipient.

tax return

A formal statement reporting taxable activity to an authority.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A customer pays $110 for a $100 product. Where did that extra $10 actually go, and does the business get to keep it?

Sales Tax and GST/VAT Concepts

In plain words

Sales tax, GST, or VAT is a tax added to the price of goods or services, collected by the business from the customer, and then paid over to the government.

A business collecting sales tax is like a landlord collecting a tenant's utility payment to pass along to the utility company — the money passes through the business, but it was never actually the business's own money to keep.

How sales tax typically works

StepExample
Product price$100
+ Sales tax (example 10%)+ $10
= Amount customer pays$110
Business remits to government$10 (not kept as business income)

Why this matters to you

Sales tax collected from customers is NOT business income and should never be recorded or spent as if it were — it's a liability owed to the government the moment it's collected, which is exactly why it needs its own separate, clearly tracked account.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a product costs $200 before tax, and the sales tax rate is 15%, calculate the total price the customer pays.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Sales tax / VAT / GSTA tax added to a sale's price, collected from customers and paid to the government
RemitTo pass collected tax money along to the government
Study tip: Always keep collected sales tax in a clearly separate account, mentally treating it as money that already belongs to the government — spending it as if it were regular business income is a common and serious mistake.

lessons.title: 13.5 Withholding Tax
lessons.html:
Withholding TaxLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Withholding Tax

Withholding Tax is the focus of this Taxation Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to maintain tax records and understand basic filing responsibilities.

tax

A compulsory payment imposed by government.

withholding tax

Tax deducted at source before payment reaches the recipient.

tax return

A formal statement reporting taxable activity to an authority.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business pays a contractor for services. Does it hand over the full agreed amount, or does something get deducted first, before the contractor even sees it?

Withholding Tax

In plain words

Withholding tax is tax deducted at the source of a payment — like a business paying a contractor — and paid directly to the government on the recipient's behalf.

Withholding tax is like an employer collecting a small portion of a payment before it even reaches the recipient, similar to how income tax is withheld directly from an employee's wages, but applied here to payments made to contractors or suppliers.

How withholding tax typically works

StepExample
Contractor's invoice$1,000
− Withholding tax (example 5%)− $50
= Amount actually paid to contractor$950
Business remits withheld amount$50 sent directly to the government

Why this matters to you

Withholding tax shifts responsibility for collecting certain taxes onto the paying business itself — failing to withhold and remit correctly can create legal and financial risk for the business making the payment, not just the recipient.

🧪 Try it yourself: If a business pays a contractor a $2,000 invoice with a 10% withholding tax rate, calculate the amount actually paid to the contractor.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Withholding taxTax deducted at the source of a payment and paid to the government on the recipient's behalf
SourceThe point where a payment originates, where withholding tax is deducted
Study tip: Confirm exactly which types of payments require withholding tax in your specific country before making any contractor or supplier payment — the requirements and rates vary and carry real compliance responsibility for the paying business.

lessons.title: 13.6 Tax Records and Filing
lessons.html:
Tax Records and FilingLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Tax Records and Filing

Tax Records and Filing is the focus of this Taxation Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to maintain tax records and understand basic filing responsibilities.

tax

A compulsory payment imposed by government.

withholding tax

Tax deducted at source before payment reaches the recipient.

tax return

A formal statement reporting taxable activity to an authority.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Tax season arrives, and a business needs to file its return. Can it just estimate its figures, or does it need real, specific documentation?

Tax Records and Filing

In plain words

Tax records and filing means keeping organised, accurate documentation to support every figure reported on a tax return, and submitting that return correctly and on time.

Good tax record-keeping is like keeping receipts for every claim on an insurance form — without them, even a completely honest claim can be questioned, delayed, or rejected simply for lacking proper supporting evidence.

Good tax record practices

PracticeWhy it matters
Keep source documents for every transactionSupports every figure reported on the tax return
Organise records by tax periodMakes filing faster and less stressful
File on timeAvoids late penalties and interest
Retain records for the required periodAvailable if the tax authority ever asks for verification

Why this matters to you

Tax filing becomes far less stressful when it's simply the final step of an already well-organised bookkeeping system — everything covered throughout this entire course, done consistently, is what actually makes accurate, timely tax filing possible.

🧪 Try it yourself: List two source documents (from Module 2) that a business would need to keep in order to support its tax return figures.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Tax filingSubmitting a completed, accurate tax return to the relevant tax authority
Retention periodThe length of time records must legally be kept, in case of future review
Study tip: Maintain organised, complete tax records continuously throughout the year, not just when a filing deadline approaches — most of the stress in tax season comes from disorganisation that built up earlier, not the filing itself.

lessons.title: 13.7 Common Tax Mistakes to Avoid
lessons.html:
Common Tax Mistakes to AvoidLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Common Tax Mistakes to Avoid

Common Tax Mistakes to Avoid is the focus of this Taxation Basics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to maintain tax records and understand basic filing responsibilities.

tax

A compulsory payment imposed by government.

withholding tax

Tax deducted at source before payment reaches the recipient.

tax return

A formal statement reporting taxable activity to an authority.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Many businesses make the exact same handful of tax mistakes every single year. Do you already know what they are — and can you avoid them?

Common Tax Mistakes to Avoid

In plain words

This lesson covers the most frequent tax mistakes businesses make, so you can recognise and avoid them in your own bookkeeping and filing.

These common mistakes are like a few well-known potholes on an otherwise manageable road — most tax problems trace back to one of a small, predictable set of avoidable errors, not some rare, complicated issue.

Frequent tax mistakes

MistakeHow to avoid it
Mixing personal and business expensesKeep strictly separate accounts and records
Missing the filing deadlineTrack deadlines well in advance, not at the last moment
Poor record-keeping throughout the yearMaintain organised bookkeeping continuously, not just at tax time
Claiming ineligible deductionsConfirm each deduction is genuinely allowed before claiming it

Why this matters to you

Recognising these common patterns in advance turns tax compliance from an intimidating, unpredictable challenge into a manageable checklist — most real-world tax problems trace back to one of these same few, well-known, avoidable mistakes.

🧪 Try it yourself: Review your own understanding of this module and identify which ONE of these four common mistakes you'd most need to be careful about avoiding, and why.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Ineligible deductionAn expense claimed as a tax deduction that doesn't actually qualify
ComplianceCorrectly meeting all legal tax obligations
Study tip: Review this list of common mistakes periodically, especially as tax season approaches — a brief, deliberate check against these well-known pitfalls can prevent a genuinely costly and avoidable error.

lessons.title: 14.1 Sole Proprietorship Accounting
lessons.html:
Sole Proprietorship AccountingLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sole Proprietorship Accounting

Sole Proprietorship Accounting is the focus of this Accounting for Different Organizations lesson. It develops the learner's ability to adapt accounting systems to businesses, nonprofits, churches, and public institutions.

entity

An organisation treated as a separate accounting unit.

fund accounting

A system separating resources according to restrictions or purposes.

accounting policy

A principle or method chosen for preparing financial information.

🤔 Let's start with a question
One person owns a small shop. Do they still need to keep separate business accounts, or can they just track everything in their head?

Sole Proprietorship Accounting

In plain words

A sole proprietorship is a business owned by one person, and its accounting keeps the business's money completely separate from the owner's personal money, even though legally they are the same person.

Running a sole proprietorship without separate records is like mixing your grocery money with your business cash in one pocket — you can still spend it, but you will never really know if the business itself is profitable.

Key accounting features

FeatureWhat it means
Owner's CapitalMoney the owner puts into the business
DrawingsMoney or goods the owner takes out for personal use
Simple structureUsually one set of books, no shareholders or partners
Unlimited liabilityOwner is personally responsible for all business debts

Why this matters to you

Most small shops, market stalls, and freelance services in Liberia operate as sole proprietorships, so understanding this simple structure is often a bookkeeper's very first real client.

🧪 Try it yourself: List three small businesses you know personally that are run by a single owner, and note whether you think they keep separate business records.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Sole proprietorshipA business owned and run by one person
Unlimited liabilityThe owner is personally responsible for all business debts
Study tip: Even for a one-person business, always keep a separate record of what goes in and out — 'it's all my money anyway' is exactly how small businesses lose track of whether they're truly profitable.

lessons.title: 14.2 Partnership Accounting Basics
lessons.html:
Partnership Accounting BasicsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Partnership Accounting Basics

Partnership Accounting Basics is the focus of this Accounting for Different Organizations lesson. It develops the learner's ability to adapt accounting systems to businesses, nonprofits, churches, and public institutions.

entity

An organisation treated as a separate accounting unit.

fund accounting

A system separating resources according to restrictions or purposes.

accounting policy

A principle or method chosen for preparing financial information.

🤔 Let's start with a question
Two friends open a business together, each contributing different amounts of money. How does accounting keep track of what belongs to each of them?

Partnership Accounting Basics

In plain words

Partnership accounting tracks each partner's individual capital, drawings, and share of profit or loss, even though the business itself operates as one combined entity.

A partnership is like two people cooking one big pot of soup together — the soup is shared, but accounting still needs to know exactly how much each person put in and how much each should take out.

What partnership accounts track

RecordPurpose
Capital accountsEach partner's original and additional contributions
Current accountsOngoing drawings and profit share for each partner
Profit-sharing ratioAgreed percentage split of profits between partners
Partnership agreementWritten terms covering contributions, roles, and profit shares

Why this matters to you

Many small Liberian businesses start as informal partnerships between family members or friends, and disputes over money are far less likely when clear, separate accounts show exactly what each partner contributed and earned.

🧪 Try it yourself: Imagine two partners contributing $600 and $400 respectively and agreeing to split profit in that same ratio. If profit is $1,000, calculate each partner's share.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
PartnershipA business owned by two or more people who share profits and responsibilities
Profit-sharing ratioThe agreed percentage split of profit between partners
Study tip: Always put profit-sharing ratios and contribution amounts in writing from day one — verbal agreements between partners are the most common cause of business breakups.

lessons.title: 14.3 Company Accounting Basics
lessons.html:
Company Accounting BasicsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Company Accounting Basics

Company Accounting Basics is the focus of this Accounting for Different Organizations lesson. It develops the learner's ability to adapt accounting systems to businesses, nonprofits, churches, and public institutions.

entity

An organisation treated as a separate accounting unit.

fund accounting

A system separating resources according to restrictions or purposes.

accounting policy

A principle or method chosen for preparing financial information.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A business grows large enough to have dozens of shareholders who never even meet each other. How can accounting represent ownership that's split so widely?

Company Accounting Basics

In plain words

Company accounting represents ownership through shares, records profit as belonging to shareholders, and treats the company as a separate legal entity distinct from any individual owner.

A company is like a large ship owned jointly by many investors through tickets called shares — no single passenger owns the whole ship, but each share represents a small, tradeable piece of it.

Key company accounting terms

TermMeaning
Share capitalMoney raised by selling shares to shareholders
Retained earningsProfit kept in the company rather than paid out
DividendsProfit distributed to shareholders
Limited liabilityShareholders only risk what they invested, not personal assets

Why this matters to you

As Liberian businesses grow from small shops into larger registered companies, understanding share capital and limited liability becomes essential for correctly recording ownership and profit distribution.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look up one well-known company (local or international) and find out, if you can, whether it pays dividends to its shareholders.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Share capitalMoney a company raises by selling shares
Limited liabilityShareholders only risk the amount they invested, not personal assets
Study tip: Remember that a company is legally separate from its owners — this single idea explains why companies can have limited liability, keep existing after an owner sells their shares, and be sued in their own name.

lessons.title: 14.4 Nonprofit and NGO Accounting
lessons.html:
Nonprofit and NGO AccountingLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Nonprofit and NGO Accounting

Nonprofit and NGO Accounting is the focus of this Accounting for Different Organizations lesson. It develops the learner's ability to adapt accounting systems to businesses, nonprofits, churches, and public institutions.

entity

An organisation treated as a separate accounting unit.

fund accounting

A system separating resources according to restrictions or purposes.

accounting policy

A principle or method chosen for preparing financial information.

🤔 Let's start with a question
An NGO receives a large donor grant meant only for building a school. Can the organization spend that same money on anything else it needs?

Nonprofit and NGO Accounting

In plain words

Nonprofit and NGO accounting tracks funds separately by purpose and donor requirement, ensuring restricted grant money is spent only on what it was given for, unlike ordinary business profit.

NGO accounting is like managing several separate envelopes of cash, each labeled for a specific purpose — you cannot simply move money from the 'school building' envelope into the 'staff salaries' envelope, even if both are legitimate needs.

Nonprofit accounting concepts

ConceptMeaning
Restricted fundsMoney that must be used only for a specific donor-approved purpose
Unrestricted fundsMoney the organization can use for any legitimate purpose
Fund accountingTracking each funding source and its use separately
Donor reportingProviding donors proof their funds were used as agreed

Why this matters to you

Liberia has many active NGOs and community organizations, and bookkeepers who understand fund accounting and donor reporting are especially valuable to this important, fast-growing sector.

🧪 Try it yourself: If you know of a local NGO or church project, ask (respectfully) whether they keep separate records for different grants or donations, and what they report back to donors.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Restricted fundsMoney that must be used only for a specific approved purpose
Fund accountingTracking each funding source and its use separately
Study tip: Always keep restricted donor funds in clearly separate records from the very first transaction — untangling mixed funds later is far harder, and donors expect precise, honest reporting.

Church and Religious Organization AccountsLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Church and Religious Organization Accounts

Church and Religious Organization Accounts is the focus of this Accounting for Different Organizations lesson. It develops the learner's ability to adapt accounting systems to businesses, nonprofits, churches, and public institutions.

entity

An organisation treated as a separate accounting unit.

fund accounting

A system separating resources according to restrictions or purposes.

accounting policy

A principle or method chosen for preparing financial information.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A church receives regular tithes plus a special offering collected just for repairing its roof. Should both types of money be recorded the same simple way?

Church and Religious Organization Accounts

In plain words

Church and religious organization accounting tracks general offerings, tithes, and special-purpose collections separately, while maintaining transparency and accountability to the congregation.

Church accounts are like a household with a general grocery fund and a separate jar saved specifically for a family trip — mixing them makes it impossible to know if either goal is truly being met.

Common church accounting records

RecordPurpose
General offering recordRegular tithes and offerings for ongoing operations
Special fund recordMoney collected for a specific project, like building repairs
Expense recordUtilities, staff support, maintenance, and outreach costs
Financial report to congregationRegular transparent summary shared with members

Why this matters to you

Churches and religious organizations across Liberia handle significant community trust and donated funds, so simple, transparent records build lasting confidence between leadership and the congregation.

🧪 Try it yourself: Design a simple one-page template a small church could use to record weekly general offerings separately from a special building fund.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
TitheA regular contribution, often a portion of income, given to a religious organization
Special fundMoney collected and reserved for one specific purpose
Study tip: Whatever the size of the congregation, share a simple, honest financial summary regularly — trust, once damaged over money, is very difficult for any organization to rebuild.

accounting policy

A principle or method chosen for preparing financial information.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A government ministry spends taxpayer money on roads and schools. Should it track spending the same way a private company tracks profit?

Government and Public Sector Accounting Basics

In plain words

Government and public sector accounting focuses on tracking how public budgets are spent and ensuring accountability to citizens, rather than measuring private profit.

Government accounting is like managing a household budget given by neighbors who expect a full, honest report on exactly how their contributed money was spent, rather than trying to make a personal profit from it.

Key public sector accounting ideas

IdeaMeaning
BudgetA plan for how public funds will be spent over a period
Public accountabilityDuty to report honestly on the use of public funds
AppropriationFunds officially approved for a specific government purpose
AuditIndependent check that public funds were used properly

Why this matters to you

Understanding basic public sector accounting helps citizens and future government employees alike recognize what proper, transparent management of public funds should look like.

🧪 Try it yourself: Find a publicly available government or ministry budget summary (even a simplified news report) and identify one specific spending category mentioned.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
BudgetA plan for how funds will be spent over a period
Public accountabilityThe duty to report honestly on the use of public funds
Study tip: When examining any public budget, always ask: is this appropriated fund category clearly reported on later? That single question is at the heart of public accountability.

lessons.title: 14.7 Choosing the Right System for Your Organization
lessons.html:
Choosing the Right System for Your OrganizationLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Choosing the Right System for Your Organization

Choosing the Right System for Your Organization is the focus of this Accounting for Different Organizations lesson. It develops the learner's ability to adapt accounting systems to businesses, nonprofits, churches, and public institutions.

entity

An organisation treated as a separate accounting unit.

fund accounting

A system separating resources according to restrictions or purposes.

accounting policy

A principle or method chosen for preparing financial information.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A market vendor, a growing company, and a large NGO all need to keep records. Should all three use exactly the same accounting approach?

Choosing the Right System for Your Organization

In plain words

Choosing the right accounting system means matching your record-keeping method to your organization's size, structure, and legal requirements, rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach.

Choosing an accounting system is like choosing the right size vehicle for a job — a bicycle suits a small errand, a truck suits heavy cargo, and using the wrong one wastes effort or leaves the job undone.

Matching the system to the organization

Organization typeTypical accounting approach
Sole proprietorshipSimple single-owner books; cashbook and basic ledger often enough
PartnershipSeparate partner capital/current accounts alongside standard ledgers
CompanyFull double-entry system with share capital and statutory reporting
NGO or churchFund accounting to separately track restricted and general money

Why this matters to you

This entire module has shown that 'accounting' isn't one single fixed method — recognizing which structure an organization has is the first step toward setting up bookkeeping that actually fits its real needs.

🧪 Try it yourself: For each of the four organization types in the table above, name one real or imagined example from your own community.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Organization structureThe legal and ownership form a business or group operates under
Fit-for-purpose systemAn accounting approach specifically suited to an organization's size and needs
Study tip: Before setting up any client's books, first ask what type of organization they are — sole proprietorship, partnership, company, or nonprofit — since that single answer shapes everything else about the right system to use.

lessons.title: 15.1 What Are Internal Controls?
lessons.html:
What Are Internal Controls?Lesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Are Internal Controls?

What Are Internal Controls? is the focus of this Internal Controls, Auditing & Ethics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to protect assets, prevent fraud, support audits, and act ethically.

internal control

A process designed to safeguard assets and improve reliable reporting.

segregation of duties

Division of responsibilities so one person does not control every transaction stage.

audit trail

A traceable record connecting transactions to supporting evidence.

🤔 Let's start with a question
A shop owner cannot personally watch every cash transaction all day. How can the business still protect itself from mistakes and theft?

What Are Internal Controls?

In plain words

Internal controls are the rules, procedures, and checks a business puts in place to protect its assets, ensure accurate records, and prevent errors or fraud.

Internal controls are like the locks, alarms, and check-in procedures at a building's entrance — no single measure stops everything alone, but together they make problems far less likely and much easier to catch.

Common types of internal controls

TypeExample
Authorization controlsA manager must approve any purchase over a set amount
Physical controlsLocking a cash drawer or storeroom
Documentation controlsRequiring a receipt or voucher for every payment
Segregation of dutiesDifferent people handle cash, recording, and approval

Why this matters to you

Weak internal controls are one of the most common reasons small and growing businesses lose money to error or fraud without ever realizing it until it's too late — good controls catch problems early, while they're still small.

🧪 Try it yourself: List one internal control you have personally seen used at a shop, school, or organization (for example, requiring a receipt for every purchase).

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Internal controlA rule or procedure that protects assets and ensures accurate records
Segregation of dutiesDividing tasks among different people so no one person controls an entire process
Study tip: Even a very small business benefits from at least one or two simple internal controls, like requiring receipts for every payment — protection doesn't require a large, complicated system to be effective.

lessons.title: 15.2 Segregation of Duties
lessons.html:
Segregation of DutiesLesson note

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Segregation of Duties

Segregation of Duties is the focus of this Internal Controls, Auditing & Ethics lesson. It develops the learner's ability to protect assets, prevent fraud, support audits, and act ethically.

internal control

A process designed to safeguard assets and improve reliable reporting.

segregation of duties

Division of responsibilities so one person does not control every transaction stage.

audit trail

A traceable record connecting transactions to supporting evidence.

🤔 Let's start with a question
One employee alone receives cash, records it, AND approves the records. Is there anything specifically risky about that single arrangement?

Segregation of Duties

In plain words

Segregation of duties means dividing key financial tasks, like handling cash, recording transactions, and approving payments, among different people so no one person can commit and hide an error or fraud alone.

Segregation of duties is like a restaurant kitchen where one person cooks and a different person checks the bill — if the same person did both, mistakes or dishonesty would be far easier to hide.

Duties that should usually be separated

DutyShould be separate from
Handling cashRecording the transaction in the books
Recording transactionsApproving or authorizing them
Preparing bank reconciliationsHandling the actual cash or bank deposits
Ordering goodsApproving payment for those goods

Why this matters to you

Very small businesses with only one or two staff members often cannot fully separate every duty, but understanding the principle helps them add extra checks, like an owner's regular spot review, where full separation isn't possible.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of a small business you know and identify one task combination (for example, one person both buying supplies and approving the payment) that might benefit from being split between two people.

Key words to remember

WordWhat it means
Segregation of dutiesDividing tasks among different people to reduce fraud and error risk
CollusionTwo or more people secretly working together to bypass controls
Study tip: When only a few staff make full separation impossible, add a simple substitute check, like the owner spot-reviewing records monthly — some oversight is always better than none.
